item.title: The storm before the storm
item.author: 1axbilssfnjhmm40n6u442lrkqfv6jgx7vespv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: The weekend before Election Day is usually one of my favorite times.The last campaign ads have shipped, field plans are finalized and Election Day preparations are in place. The fury of last-minute charges and countercharges subsides as candidates try to deliver a positive closing message.A seriousness settles over the electorate as election officials make final preparations for voting and vote counting.For a few quiet days, the fate of the election lies solely in the voters’ hands.I normally use the time to get organized and catch up on tasks I’ve set aside. I get some sleep, knowing that Tuesday will be a long night.It is the proverbial calm before the storm that is sure to come once the polls close and states begin the process of counting ballots and certifying results.This year, however, has been different. The weekend before Election Day has been anything but quiet. It has been the storm before the storm.Even with the warnings that Donald Trump would try to rig the election, and even knowing that Attorney General Todd Blanche would carry out Trump’s every whim, I did not expect it to be this bad.Over the last few weeks, we have witnessed a daily escalation in the government’s assault on free and fair elections. In the last few days, it has reached a level never before seen in this country.Trump’s Department of Justice is trying to force election officials to set aside, or segregate, ballots it claims are suspect, and it is threatening officials who refuse to comply. It is now using the threat of criminal investigation to intimidate political opponents and their supporters.On Friday, the DOJ admitted that federal agencies had contacted officials in five states, California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Washington, about voters it claims are ineligible to vote in the midterms.The DOJ also revealed that it had sent letters to election officials in all 50 states, warning that they could face prison time if they do not preserve voting records for 22 months after the election.In Alaska, the DOJ has asked a federal judge to order election officials to segregate ballots based on which candidate a voter cast their ballot for. This is a lawsuit Donald Trump has said he ordered filed.It asserts powers the federal government does not possess. It tramples on the right of states to run their own elections and makes a mockery of the Constitution.Yet Trump’s loyal foot soldiers filed it, and they have been bobbing and weaving ever since to avoid a ruling on motions to dismiss their frivolous case.Now they have loudly announced a criminal investigation in the days leading up to the election.I am not going to bother pointing out the DOJ’s policy against this type of action. Nor will I dwell on the fact that the U.S. attorney seemed unable to articulate what the potential crime would be.Instead, I will only ask why so few are willing to speak out about what they know is happening.In the depths of the struggle for civil rights, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that “the greatest tragedy of this period of social transition was not the strident clamor of the bad people, but the appalling silence of the good people.”Now, as we head into Election Day, the question is not whether good people remain. It is whether they will ever speak out.Instead, they prefer to act like nothing is really that different. This is just another election.Acknowledging the depth of the crisis would require large law firms to defend the rule of law instead of sitting on the sidelines. It would force corporate titans to speak out instead of cutting deals with Trump. It would make the legacy media confront how their fixation on both-sides coverage has damaged their reputation and failed their profession.Instead, they all pretend this is a normal election when it is anything but. Better to feign ignorance than to confirm their complicity.In the coming days, the storm will grow. Donald Trump will escalate his attacks even further. That is what he has done before.He may disrupt voting or demand more meritless lawsuits and baseless prosecutions. He might insist that ballots be seized and election certifications set aside. He might even try to declare some sort of national emergency.What he won’t be able to do is change people’s hearts and minds. He can try to rig the maps, suppress the vote and subvert the results, but he cannot change the fact that he and his party are deeply unpopular and that they will lose this election.I don’t know how big the blue wave will be or how many Republicans will be washed out when this storm finally breaks.What I am certain of is that once the election is over, we must stop the DOJ from being used as a tool of naked partisan aggression. And we must insist that more people who claim to be good speak out before the next storm arrives.

item.title: Saturday 80s Jam: How Will I Know – Whitney Houston
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: When Whitney Houston released “How Will I Know” in 1985, she was still in the early stages of what would become one of the most extraordinary careers in pop music. Her debut album had already produced “You Give Good Love,” but “How Will I Know” was the song that showed the world just how perfectly her enormous voice could fit into bright, energetic 1980s pop.Written by George Merrill, Shannon Rubicam, and Narada Michael Walden, the song was originally intended for another artist. Houston’s version transformed it into something much bigger. Produced by Michael Walden, the recording combined synthesizers, electronic drums, handclaps, keyboards, and a relentlessly upbeat rhythm that was almost impossible to sit still through.That was a major departure from the more serious image often associated with powerhouse vocalists.Houston could obviously sing a huge ballad, but “How Will I Know” demonstrated that she could also have fun.The song is essentially about romantic uncertainty. Houston is interested in someone but doesn’t know whether the feelings are mutual. Instead of treating that uncertainty as something dramatic and depressing, the song turns it into a burst of nervous energy.The production is a huge part of that feeling.The drums bounce along, the keyboards sparkle, the backing vocals reinforce the chorus, and Houston’s voice cuts through the arrangement with astonishing clarity. She doesn’t have to overpower the production. She simply sits perfectly on top of it.Directed by Brian Grant, the “How Will I Know” video was filled with bright colors, geometric sets, dancers, energetic choreography, and unmistakable mid-1980s fashion. It was tailor-made for MTV, which was rapidly becoming one of the most important promotional forces in popular music.Houston’s image in the video was youthful, stylish, and playful.She wasn’t being presented solely as a serious vocalist standing behind a microphone. She was a pop star.The song became Houston’s second number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100 and helped turn her debut album into a massive success. It also established a formula that would define much of her early career: combine an extraordinary voice with sophisticated pop production and make the result accessible to virtually anyone.“How Will I Know” is particularly impressive because Houston never sounds like she’s struggling to fit into the upbeat production.She sounds completely natural.Her vocal runs add personality without overwhelming the melody, while the chorus gives her plenty of room to show off the power that would eventually become her trademark.The song also captures something essential about 1980s pop. This was the decade when electronic production, MTV, fashion, dance music, and traditional vocal performances increasingly came together.“How Will I Know” sits right in the middle of that cultural shift.It sounds unmistakably like 1985, but its melody is strong enough that the song never feels trapped in its era.Most importantly, it helped establish Whitney Houston as something more than a promising new singer.She was becoming a superstar.Over the next several years, Houston would deliver enormous ballads, blockbuster movie songs, and some of the most recognizable recordings in popular music.But “How Will I Know” remains special because it captures her at the beginning of that journey.Young, energetic, impossibly talented, and surrounded by one of the decade’s most infectious productions, Whitney Houston turned a song about wondering whether someone liked her into a celebration of the excitement of not knowing.And the answer, judging by the success of the song, was pretty obvious.Everybody was going to know Whitney Houston.

item.content:encoded: Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.

item.title: Let’s Talk About Alaska
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I was at the gym this afternoon when a press conference came on with the U.S. Attorney in Alaska floridly introducing a criminal investigation into this “Dan Sullivan” issue in Alaska. One of my colleagues just noted that to do this, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman “unrecused” himself from this case. “Unrecusal” is not a thing. He recused himself because he’s trying to get a judgeship from Alaska’s Republican senators Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski. I note this simply for the comedic nature of this spectacle. This investigation is itself a corrupt abuse of power on three or four different grounds at once.Let me share some thoughts on this.I’ve heard a number of people say they’re “troubled” or “disturbed” or unhappy that this happened. All I can say is that I would really recommend that you toughen up because you simply won’t make it through the next few years, even under the best circumstances. There is no crime here and no possibility of a crime here. This is trolling. At worst, it’s a dirty trick. If it is a dirty trick it is a special kind since it has been out in the open and has been a staple of Alaska political news for the better part of a year. Election officials in Alaska already took note of the possibility of confusion and added the word “incumbent” after Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s name on the ballot, as well as “registered Republican” to make certain that no one can be confused as to who is who. State authorities are the only ones permitted to judge this question and arrive at a solution to it, if it requires one. They already have.

item.title: Royals Off-Season Report
item.author: SRS0=xjif=IU=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: Although the Royals season mercifully ended a few weeks ago, the 2026 major league season concluded this week with the Milwaukee Brewers winning their first World Series title in franchise history 4 games to 1 over the Tampa Bay Rays.The crowning of a World Series champion signifies the official start to the MLB off-season. With a lockout of the players looming on Dec. 1, the next few weeks are bound to be jammed full of MLB news. Some of it might even involve the Royals!This means that Alec Marsh’s time in the organization has come to an end. It really looked like he could be in the rotation for some time in 2024, but injuries derailed his career and he hasn’t pitched in over two years now. Alex Lange’s time with his hometown team did not go as either had hoped. He finished with a 6.75 ERA and 1.63 WHIP across 60 innings of work. I’m sure he’ll get another shot somewhere. Gonsolin had some decent years with the Dodgers before getting hurt, but this smacks of desperation. Then again, “desperate” might be the best word to describe the Royals starting pitching situation going into 2027.It’s been fairly quiet on the rumor front, but a few are starting to circulate around the Royals.Look, it’s not going to happen. The Royals aren’t going to trade Bobby Baseball. That said, if I’m Picollo and the Red Sox actually make this offer…I take it. Vinnie, Massey, and of course Bobby were consistently excellent, but Loftin? Really? His defense at third is better than at second, but I’m not sure it is Gold Glove caliber. Winners will be announced Sunday evening on ESPN.Beginning next Tuesday (11/3), teams can start signing free agents and making trades. Remember that is a process that sometimes lasts the entire three months of a normal off-season. With the impending lockout on Dec. 2nd, teams will have to cram all of their acquisitions into less than a month. It’s hard for me to fit my brain around the idea of signing some guy to a gazillion dollar contract when you don’t even know the rules the game is going to be played under next season. Will there be a salary cap? A salary floor? Will there even be a season in 2027?

item.title: Manchester United And Michael Carrick Are Breaking New Ground In Organizational Dysfunction
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: There are few joys in sports that can truly exceed a game in which both coaches are in danger of getting fired, and no place does that game better than England. There are no distractions that can cause the fevered punditocracy to avert its eyes from the desperate hope that one (or, in the most orgiastic case, both) gets smoked right after the game. This is possible because a dissatisfying draw can enrage both fan bases equally, in the way that Giants-Commanders sickened the souls of football fans on this side of the ditch three weeks ago.But there is one scenario that trumps even that, and Americans will have it tomorrow morning at the breakfast hour: Manchester United at Chelsea. Two big clubs that are underachieving in their own specific ways, will face each other at 8:30 a.m. ET, and in deepest zombie hours on the West Coast. What makes it genuinely special for everyone is that no institution on earth, in any pursuit, does boss-in-trouble quite like Manchester United.Carrick got the full car wash a week ago after successive three-goal losses to Como (4-1) in the Champions League and Bournemouth (3-0) in the Prem. This extended a stretch of winless results that go back to United's Champions League win over Sabah of Azerbaijan, a newbie team that, on the European stage, qualifies not as minnows but something more on the order of plankton. The first loss was in Italy, in a very cool stadium that overlooks Lake Como, and which by definition is the coolest stadium in Europe because of it. The second was at home before—get this—an appreciative crowd that applauded Carrick when the team went for the postgame salute to the fans. They turned unanimously loud, profane, and ugly as soon as Carrick left the field.

item.title: Three-Body Orbits
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: There are no generalized solutions to the three-body problem. Say you have three planets orbiting each other: it’s impossible to calculate how they will move using Newton’s laws of motion and gravity.Unlike the two-body problem, the three-body problem has no general closed-form analytic solution. The differential equations that govern the motions of three gravitating bodies are not integrable and cannot be solved to give explicit formulas for the positions of the bodies as a function of time. For most initial conditions, the dynamical system for three orbiting bodies is chaotic, and the only way to predict their motions is to estimate them using numerical methods.The site even enables you to search for new stable solutions to the problem in your browser. This is what one of my unsuccessful tests looked like — two of the planets locked in a gravity death spiral while the other one peaces out in the other direction:

item.title: Darius Acuff Jr. Is A Problem, But Which Kind?
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: During the first quarter of Thursday's game between the equally winless Pelicans and Kings, Sacramento rookie Darius Acuff Jr. ran the length of the floor in transition and punched home a sweeping dunk past a late trail from Jeremiah Fears and a halfhearted contest from Trey Murphy III. It was an amazing play, which is why Acuff took a second to flex and mean-mug for the dozens of fans in New Orleans. It was also a live play, and as Acuff preened, the Pelicans ran back and Murphy got an easy dunk, after Acuff's absence forced Domantas Sabonis to abandon the paint.This sequence serves as a useful Rorschach test for the Acuff observer: Do you see Acuff's smooth athleticism, and his ability to produce not only tough but beautiful buckets? Or do you see an undersized guard whose lack of interest in the floor game is matched only by his inability to affect it? Both are totally valid reads of the most (and only) fascinating player on the worst team in basketball, although I think partisans of both positions would agree that Acuff's first five NBA games have been remarkable.Nobody in the league has attempted or missed more shots. No rookie has attempted as many shots in their first few games. Acuff sits snugly wedged between Steph Curry and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander on the usage leaderboard, with the sixth-highest rate in the NBA. It's both fantastic theater and an irresistible new front in the Real Hooper Wars; the Kings, in the meantime, are so bad that the question of any of it mattering will be entirely theoretical for a while. This leaves us all free to enjoy Acuff's game and use it as a plank from which to mount arguments about how basketball should work.

item.title: Poll-mageddon—Kansas Edition!
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: WaPo published a fascinating piece this morning tied to their latest poll of Kansas. The headline, figurative if not literal, is that they came up with a result that shows incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall not behind Adam Hamilton, but way behind. But they don’t buy their own result. What’s fascinating and laudable is that polls like this, this late in the cycle, often never get released or they get adjusted to bring them more into line with pollsters’ expectations or the consensus of other polls. But here the Post made the decision to release the poll as is and pull back the veil on all the internal details and decisions they made to get the poll as close to what they think is accurate as they could.Differential response has been the bane of pollsters for more than a decade. We know that no one answers the phone (or the text message) when pollsters get in touch anymore. The problem is that Republicans and Democrats “never” respond at slightly different rates. And even more specifically, the slice of usually disaffected voters that Donald Trump has repeatedly activated when he’s on the presidential ballot are the most poll-resistant of all. So a huge amount of what has happened in the polling industry over the last decade is pollsters trying to find ways to tweak numbers in some coherent way to adjust for getting too few of those poll-shy Trump voters. (And to be clear, this isn’t the old idea that they’re embarrassed to say they support Trump. They just don’t want to talk to pollsters.) Further complicating the issue is that that activation — and the polling misses tied to it — doesn’t seem to happen in midterm elections, based on 2018 and 2022.

item.title: ‘The Devils’ Gets Its Due
item.author: Corey Atad
item.content:encoded: Aldous Huxley likened the exorcism of the prioress Jeanne des Anges to “a rape in a public lavatory.” It was this horrific description that director Ken Russell shared with production designer Derek Jarman before they set out to tell that story. Russell wanted to capture the spirit of Huxley’s nonfiction book, , about the 17th-century incident in which a convent of nuns claimed possession, exhibiting wild and lewd behavior, leading to the sorcery conviction and execution of the priest Urbain Grandier. For that 1971 adaptation, , Jarman took the assignment quite literally. Large, white tiles cover every inch of Loudun’s Ursuline convent in the film, from floor to wall to arched ceiling. Tiles, and iron bars. It’s a gorgeous set, photographed by cinematographer David Watkin in anamorphic widescreen grandeur, and immerses the audience in the suffocated, cloistered lives of the nuns. Its starkness is at once mesmerizing and maddening. It is the perfect place for a case of possession—or many—and a likely site for clinically staged abuse.This wasn’t the first time I’d seen the scene in question, which is somehow more and less disturbing than Huxley’s six words suggests. I first watched some 15 or 20 years ago, on a pirated copy. It was a film whose reputation preceded it, and I was a young guy, barely out of high school, titillated by its scandalous history. Even before it was originally released, was heavily cut to appease British censors. It was cut further still for its American release. Though it earned respectable sums at the U.K. box office, the lavish Warner Bros. production received a critical thrashing—Roger Ebert’s sarcastic review is a classic in the genre of getting it completely backward—and essentially buried thereafter, popping up on a couple of VHS releases in the ’80s, but never on DVD or Blu-ray. In the early 2000s, British film critic Mark Kermode rediscovered the censored footage, helping Russell put together a director’s cut that screened only once, off a DigiBeta tape. The copy I’d watched years ago was an earlier cut, likely the original theatrical version minus the most controversial scenes, but all that history had me primed for an outrageous film, and an outrageous film is very much what I got. Sister Jeanne’s exorcism—set in that white, tiled lavatory of a convent, molested by priests wielding giant syringes to perform forced enemas—was sensational, as was the rest of the film’s high-toned lunacy. Rampant nudity, violence, actors gesticulating wildly, saying things like, “They say they can stand up to the Church, but they can't stand up to this bitch.” A movie for sickos. I loved it, naturally, but I don’t think I took it very seriously.

item.title: DOJ Election Interference Turns Into Raw Thuggery
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: I have the same mix of feelings that I did in the days leading up to Jan. 6, 2021: a queasy feeling that things are about to spiral out of control along with the recognition that it could end up just being a clown show.The Justice Department’s corrupt, heavy-handed, intimidation tactics of issuing grand jury subpoenas to election officials in California while launching a wave of new election-related subpoenas in Alaska is a level of thuggery we haven’t seen before and a grave threat.The only more direct and dramatic interference in free and fair elections would be blocking voter access to the polls, seizing ballots, and refusing to abide by the results of the election. Stay tuned, I guess?And yet there remains an unmistakable clownish quality to the whole endeavor, such as Attorney General Todd Blanche personally charging four misdemeanor cases in Nevada for alleged noncitizen voting, presumably because the top federal prosecutor in the state is implicated in the Trump U.S. attorney scheme and was disqualified.It is, as always, both/and.Trump DOJ Ignores Judges WarningIn California, the Trump DOJ reportedly made the decision to target election officials themselves with a new round of grand jury subpoenas, Bloomberg reports:Justice Department leadership directed top federal prosecutors in California to pursue criminal subpoenas of state and local officials regarding their roles administering allegedly illegal voting, according to two people familiar with the situation.This is different from earlier grand jury subpoenas in recent weeks that were directed at obtaining voting records to prosecute alleged noncitizen voting. The new subpoenas are going directly to election officials who are in the midst of counting votes and managing an election.The new subpoenas aren’t limited just to Los Angeles County: “All four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation,” the AP reported.The subpoenas come after acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to election officials in every California county earlier this month warning that they faced potential criminal prosecution for counting the ballots of alleged noncitizen voters — an unprecedented interpretation of federal criminal law.Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, echoed those threats in court this week.U.S. District Judge David O. Carter warned from the bench Tuesday that DOJ’s threats against election officials needed to “cease immediately.”In his order rejecting the Trump DOJ’s request that he order Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count alleged mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, Judge Carter warned DOJ again: “The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop.”The next day came with word of the new round of subpoenas.Conflicting Reports on Timing of SubpoenasNot all of the reporting is consistent as to when subpoenas were issued and served. But it appears that some subpoenas of election workers went out as early as last week.“At least two employees of Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week for a proceeding scheduled for Nov. 4, on the morning after the election,” the NYT reported.Three subpoenas to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder were sent Oct. 21 and 24, according to the AP, which obtained copies of them:The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. … They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted.Those subpoenas predate the new wave of subpoenas that reportedly began yesterday in all four federal district in California.Again, the focus of these latest subpoenas is different than a separate batch of prior subpoenas that focused on getting voting records in order to prosecute individual voters for allegedly being noncitizens. One such subpoena was received by Orange County election officials yesterday, adding to the confusion.Grand jury subpoenas days before the election is intimidation enough, but there was at least one extra twist: “Federal marshals served one county employee at home, despite having already served that employee at the registrar’s office and issuing a notification of counsel, according to officials familiar with the incident,” the NYT reports.“Threats and intimidation have no place in elections,” said Dean Logan, the top election official in Los Angeles County.Wave of Subpoenas in AlaskaFurther seizing on the NYT report that tied the candidacy of the Dan Sullivan to the Senate campaign of Mary Peltola, the Trump DOJ issued a wave of new subpoenas ostensibly to investigate what it claims is a conspiracy to deceive voters — but which is in reality a last-ditch effort to save a key incumbent Republican senator.“Federal prosecutors issued more than 40 grand jury subpoenas and record preservation notices to key targets by [Wednesday] evening, one of the officials said,” according to CNN, which reported that additional subpoenas were expected yesterday.There had already been a quiet federal investigation of the Sullivan candidacy before the NYT story, with some grand jury subpoenas issued and witnesses interviewed, CNN reported:The investigation had already roiled the US Attorney’s office in Alaska, one of the officials said, where some career prosecutors have balked at aspects of the probe and whether the effort broke federal law or simply represents electioneering dirty tricks.It seems clear now that the NYT report embarrassed officials at Main Justice since the newspaper story went farther than its own investigation had.In a move I’ve never seen before, the Alaska U.S. attorney Michael Heyman “un-recused” himself from the case after the NYT report at the urging of Main Justice, CNN reported. Heyman had previously recused himself early in the probe because he was in discussions with Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski about being nominated for a federal judgeship.The prosecutor-in-chief made clear his intentions soon after the NYT story broke: “I think they should be prosecuted,” President Trump said. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level.”Trump: Why Is MY Beak Dry?!?Special Weekend Morning MemoKeep an eye on your inbox for a special weekend edition of Morning Memo.With the campaigns chugging to the finish line and Trump election interference in full swing, Morning Memo will bring you the latest. Stay tuned …

item.title: Russia Is Coming Back To International Hockey
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Russia, which has been functionally banned from international hockey for more than four years, must be allowed to return to international events starting in December in Canada. That's the ruling today by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the highest sport court in the land. But there's a whole lot still unsettled, including a looming shitshow at next year's World Championships.The International Ice Hockey Federation banned the Russian member association in February 2022, as did almost every other sport's Olympic federation following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. That war is still ongoing, but in July of this year the IOC lifted its blanket ban on Russian Olympic committees, and said that its recommendations to individual sport federations no longer apply. Ukraine is currently appealing that decision.(This is tricky business, and I'm glad it's not up to me to decide. Should individual athletes be punished for their government's actions? Or is a ban of Russia's prestigious hockey program more accurately a punishment of the country as a whole? But then, why Russia and not some other war-starting, international law-ignoring countries I could name and/or live in?)

item.title: Rudimentary Lathe comes out of retirement for the 3rd time
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: I miss when a bunch of us weirdos overshared on our TiddlyWikis nearly every day. Most are gone or unmaintained now. Can we bring them back? I'll start: rudimentarylathe.orgNearly 5,000 notes going back to 2018, and man oh man, at least 4,800 of them are an embarrassment. I should keep this stuff to myself, but that horse left the barn long ago.We used to write "TiddlyMails" to each other (I don't think we actually called them that). I'd write a note that simply mentioned someone with their own wiki. They'd read it, and write a note on their wiki with a link back and a title something like: "Re: That thing you wrote". It was completely manual and done without pings or notifications of any kind. So fun!If you have a similar wiki, let me know. I'd love to visit!TiddlyWiki is more than 20 years old and still a miracle to me.

item.title: President Rottinghands McCankles cancels his remaining rallies. What a fucking loser.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Yesterday evening, out of the clear blue and without warning, the White House abruptly announced that all of Dear Leader’s upcoming weekend rallies had been canceled — fuckity-bye, hit the bricks, sayonara — thereby depriving his remaining cultists the opportunity to sit uncomfortably on a folding chair in a thimble-sized gymnasium, and listen to Donny ramble incoherently for two entire hours about how he successfully pointed at the drawing of the camel, all while being drowned out by an endless series of hecklers.Reporter Jacob Bogage: “So you not going to Kansas has nothing to do with you being sick of traveling?”Donny: “Oh, you’re sick to ask that question. You are sick. Who are you with?”Bogage: Donny: “You are a sick guy. Reuters is terrible. Can you imagine? Look at this guy. He’s way out of shape. Look at how bent— he comes [makes accordion hands] he comes to me. ‘Sir, you’re not gonna go to Kansas.’ I’m not going to Kansan because he’s doing very well. We’re gonna do a tele-rally’ … but he says, ‘you’re not going to Kansas, sir, are you feeling well?’ You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”Wow, Dear Leader sure gets cranky when he’s got a full load in his diaper — and he didn’t even hear the question correctly. Did you catch that? The reporter asks Donny if he’s and Donny goes ballistic because all he hears is And he automatically explodes into some infantile rant about ‘I’m not sick, you’re sick’ — because he’s got the emotional maturity of a four-year-old.Maybe Donny needs to get his ears checked. Is this a piece of your brain, Donny?Dear Leader can’t hack it any more. He’s too old and tired and demented to be flying across the country every single goddamned day. Plus, he’s fed up. He loves the crowds — only this time around, there aren’t any crowds. All that remains are the die-hard, brain-deadest cultists — and there aren’t even enough of them left to fill the pint-sized high school gyms his flunkies are booking him into. How long before Donny has to open for a‘Oh Natty, you’re the only one who understands me.’ I think I just threw up in my own mouth a little.So now, if you’re a cultist and you need your Donny fix this weekend, you’re going to have to zoom in to some ‘tele-rally,’ and watch Dear Leader sitting behind the Resolute Desk, drooling all over himself as he gradually loses consciousness. It’ll be just like a real rally, except you won’t be able to smell the farts.Meanwhile, let’s go live to Republican National Headquarters for the GOP’s reaction to Donny having canceled his remaining rallies.“Sources say, though, that some Republican officials are relieved by the president’s decision to cancel those final two rallies. One top Republican official told my colleague Jeff Zeleny, quote, ‘thank God. He hasn’t moved the needle anywhere.’ And a second official, saying, quote, ‘everyone has seen the president who wants to see him.’”Boo fucking hoo, Republicans. Maybe it was a mistake to hitch your wagons to an increasingly-befuddled fascist who, thanks to an increasing fog of dementia and untreated tertiary syphilis, no longer has any idea which end is up.Reporter: “Have you heard that Lt. General Sylvia leaked classified information at the Pentagon?”Reporter: “I said, Lt. General Sylvia leaked classified information at the Pentagon.”Donny: “ got problems. gonna have big problems. did. We’re very much looking for leakers, and uh—gonna have big problems.”Surely, Donny can’t be this seriously misinformed, can he?Spoiler alert: yes he can be this misinformed. Remember, Donny’s daily intel briefing has been boiled to down to a single page of bullet points and burlesque photos from the 1940s.That’s the only thing that will hold Donny’s attention. So he hasn’t a fucking clue who Lt. General Sylvia is. All he hears is the name ‘Sylvia’ and away he goes, blithering about the retribution he’s going to inflict on some imaginary woman who doesn’t exist. I’m so old, I remember when Job Biden would occasionally stumble over someone’s name, and would have to correct himself. The press would have a field day, and start filling editorial pages with piece after piece about how Sleepy Joe was too old and icky and smelly do to his job, and how he needs to step down, right now, for the good of the country.Now we have an actual cognitively-collapsed president concocting fairy tales about strange generals, lying in ponds, distributing leaks — and not one worthless scribbler of the corporate-controlled press can be bothered to say one word about it.It’s so embarrassing to have a President of the United States who is an uninformed fool who has no fucking clue what’s going on inside his own government, and just makes shit up on the spot, based on what’s he’s But tell me once again how it was Joe Biden who was the real problem. That’s such an awesome story.I swear, I yam disgustipated. Fox News bobblehead: “Tom, why are you here this morning?”Tom: “Well, in the late 70s, I was a little too young to get involved and go to South America for the Jonestown Massacre. But this is as close as I’ll ever get, so that’s why I’m here.”Bobblehead: “Wait, the Jonestown Massacre?”Tom: “That’s right. There’s nothing like seeing a cult right up front, man.”Bobblehead: “Maybe this is not a Trump supporter [walks away dejectedly]And right there, that’s your problem for Fox news — and for all the wingnut media right now. When there are too few cultists in the crowd, it’s way too easy for any mischief-maker to walk up to the dude holding the microphone, and go Masterful job, bro. Norway will be in touch to let you know when you can pick up your Nobel Trolling Prize.[Oh, and that scream you just heard, that was me — because this is where I was in writing this post when I got the notification on my phone about Donny going ahead with the canceled rallies. I was this fucking close, man.]Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here are three photos off the same roll of film from the early 1990s. First, we have Ms Spouse setting up a slide for Katie, in our back yard.Second, Ms Spouse in a hotel room in Plymouth, MA.And lastly, Katie and her mom, on the beach in Plymouth.Have a great Friday, everyone. May you have better timing than me, when news is breaking.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Na, Site Search!
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: After years in the making (or more accurately, years in the wanting), I finally figured out how I wanted to do search for KDO posts. I’ve been tinkering with this specific implementation since the beginning of the summer and it finally all came together. If you’re a member, please help me to kick the tires on this for a few days. (That link, as well as the search links below, will 404 for non-members for now.)Hopefully it’s pretty close and then I can open it up to everyone. I’ve been using it for the past week or two and it’s been really helpful so far, especially in surfacing older posts about topics I’m currently writing about or generally interested in. The tag pages are good for that too, but search can help hone in on specifics — like posts I’ve made about fascism or posts that link to McSweeney’s. Search also pulls in results from Quick Links, which aren’t included on tag pages. The rankings still need some work here and there (it’s not magic), but your searches will help calibrate things.For now, the search only looks at posts from 2014 to the present. You can search by keyword, describe what you remember (“the guy who walks in Japan”), or paste a link to find posts that link to it. Search is fuzzy-ish but it’s not an AI bot or anything like that so if you ramble on with a 25-word query, it’s probably not going to work that well. You can sort by best match or newest, search all posts or just Quick Links or main posts, and filter by time (past month, past 3 months, etc.)I’ll share more about how search works in a subsequent post. For now, kick the tires and let me know what you think in the comments or via email. As always, bug reports, comments, and suggestions are welcome.

item.title: Welcome to the offseason
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: With the World Series over and the Milwaukee Brewers the rightful champions, it’s time to end my annual postseason sabbatical. After all this time, and as the cliché goes, I hope this edition of the newsletter finds you well.Even though we’re yet to November, I plan on pacing myself as much as possible to keep the newsletter productive during what is shaping up to be a lengthy lockout once the current CBA expires on December 1. When the owners lockout the players (an unnecessary move at this point in the process), the baseball world will grind to a halt. Sadly, we’ve seen this movie before, so we know the baseball desert that awaits. The Winter Meetings will be cancelled. There will be few or no negotiating sessions though the holidays. The urgency will return when we should have camps opening in February.It’s going to be a colder winter than usual. As for what I plan to do here, there will be some player profiles, some random (i.e. wrong) free agent guesses and, of course, I'll cover any news that happens over the next month ahead of the lockout. Along with the usual baseball foolishness. So hit that subscribe button if you haven't so we can make this offseason journey together.The first order now that the offseason is officially underway is for teams to massage their 40-man roster. There will probably be a flurry of activity ahead of the lockout and for now at least, it's business as usual. The Royals saw Jonathan India, Craig Kimbrel, Luke Maile and Josh Rojas officially become free agents on Thursday. On Monday, this quartet will be free to negotiate with the rest of the teams in the league. I can’t imagine a scenario where any of these guys will be back with the Royals.Late Thursday, word came down that Carlos Estévez will soon join them on the market as the Royals declined his $13 million club option. They’ll hand over $2 million instead as a buyout. Estévez recorded one out all year and gave up a walkoff grand slam. It wasn't what anyone was looking for.Tony Gonsolin, who signed a major league contract in August and also appeared in one game for the Royals, had his 2027 option picked up. His outing was in September against the White Sox where he looked good for two innings before the wheels came off in his third frame of work. Still, you could see some of that old magic that made him appealing to the Royals. For next season, the oft-injured pitcher will be officially on the books for $2.5 million, although there are reports he can earn up to $6 million in performance incentives. Once the Royals move their players off the 60-day IL, the Royals will have 38 players on the 40-man roster.What did you think of the postseason? Overall I thought it was fine, helped by the fact the Brewers and the Rays won their respective leagues. I also low-key enjoyed the fact that the higher seeded team won every matchup in every round. Underdogs are fun, but seeing good teams advance is satisfying. My only issue: The dominance of the Milwaukee nine removed any semblance of drama from these last couple of weeks. They are such a complete ballclub that this October felt akin to 1984 when the Detroit Tigers steamrolled to victory or 1989 when it was the Oakland A’s getting down to business after coming up short the year before. While nothing is ever certain in these playoffs, especially with the expanded format, but once the Brewers started throwing haymakers at the Dodgers in the NLCS, it all seemed settled.A couple of stray World Series thoughts as we process a long winter (and probably spring) ahead...I felt the similarities between the Brewers and the 2015 Royals in that both teams played a form of what I’ve taken to call Total Baseball in that they do just about everything right. Strong starting pitching? Check. A selfless move-the-line batting order? Uh-huh. A lockdown bullpen? For sure. Clutch hits, including home runs? Yep. Hell, both teams check the box with salt of the earth managers who are refreshingly honest.There was a moment in the dying moments of the NLCS where the broadcast was doing the obligatory crowd shots and found a woman who looked like she was about to pass out. It was a combination of stress and disbelief. It was the most relatable thing I saw all October, making me think of when I had to take a seat while in the upper tank at The K for Game Four of the 2014 ALCS. I seemed to have gotten a bit lightheaded. When something is unfolding in front of you that you never, ever thought would happen, it can hit hard. I sure she rallied and partied in an appropriate manner.As we know, winning a championship after suffering through years of heartache makes the moment all the sweeter.As a self-proclaimed broadcast geek, I have to wonder why American broadcasting networks hate their viewers so much. After a summer spent watching the World Cup on Univision to dodge the audio assault from Fox soccer announcers, I found myself regularly wondering if we really need nine innings (or more) of John Smoltz who was seemingly getting paid by the word? No, we don’t and I found myself often wishing he would just shut up. There are moments where he does bring up an interesting point or two regarding strategy and whatnot, but for the most part in this World Series he was shockingly unprepared. Fox does a huge disservice by having him on the broadcast. Maybe someday TBS will get the rights to the World Series and they can have Brian Anderson, Ron Darling and Jeff Francoeur on the call. Anderson, the Brewers TV guy when not on national assignments is a pro. Darling is part of the best booth in baseball for the Mets. And Frenchy is really, really good at providing commentary to the point that I wish we could’ve enticed him to stay in Kansas City at the end of his career.I’m not surprised the early television ratings for the World Series were, while down, better than expected. While the five games weren’t exactly what I would call crisp baseball, even casual fans can appreciate when the two best teams in the game face off for the championship. It also helps that both teams embraced the moment and seemed to just have fun playing the game.Speaking of the keep-the-line-moving mentality of the Milwaukee lineup, I’m going to be thinking about the fifth inning of Game Three for a long, long time. It was epic baseball, a symphony of exit velocity, launch angle and perfectly placed hits. In an October with close games and seemingly few extended rallies, this inning was unforgettable.I know newspapers are struggling for survival, but I can’t help but continue to be disappointed by the lack of baseball coverage provided by the Kansas City Star. It wasn’t difficult to come up with a local angle with Grain Valley’s Jacob Misiorowski and Park Hill’s Aaron Ashby both playing key rolls for the Brewers. They should’ve sent someone to cover this Series.Remember when we had Andy McCullough writing about the Royals at The Star? He had the World Series wrap for The Athletic. It is, as you would expect, exceptional.As McCullough points out, the Brewers have not had an easy road even though they’ve qualified for October in eight of the last nine seasons. They’ve made several trades along the way of key players including pitchers Josh Hader, Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Not all of those deals yielded players who landed on their postseason roster. They filled the gaps through a strong international presence, outstanding scouting and exceptional drafts. It’s not an easy blueprint to replicate, but when you look at what Milwaukee General Manager Matt Arnold has done on the trade front, you have to wonder about how the Royals have failed to capitalize on peak return on some players they should’ve dealt. Missed opportunities equal missed postseasons.

item.title: Diehard Reds Blogger Spends His Office Hours Making Life Hell For Asylum Seekers
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: Judge Chadwick Dotson works out of the Charlotte Immigration Court, where he was appointed this past March. For a person to accept an appointment to the immigration court system—from the Trump administration, in the post-Minneapolis world—they have to be the person that you are imagining right now. In most ways, Dotson is exactly that. Prior to accepting this appointment—to a powerful position in one of the cruelest arms of the most blatantly criminal federal government in American history—Dotson was being sued as director of the Virginia Department of Corrections, where he was appointed by former Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin. Before that, he was chairman of the Virginia Parole Board, also under Youngkin, where he ran an ostentatiously blunt and unyielding parole operation.All along, when he isn't doling out excessive punishment or denying asylum seekers, this immigration judge is something of a regular sports blogger.Dotson writes columns about the Cincinnati Reds, his favorite baseball team, for , under the byline Chad Dotson. On Oct. 6, a little over a week after the Reds wrapped up a disappointing 75-87 campaign, Dotson pondered whether it was time for fans to step away from the team. It was the 15th article that Dotson published for the magazine that season. He has co-written a book about the MLB team, and also has a Substack newsletter called The Riverfront, where he covers the Reds and other Cincinnati sports teams. (The Riverfront occasionally dabbles in movie coverage; in his year-end list for 2023, Dotson listed Killers of the Flower Moon and among his favorite films.) On April 22, Dotson was enjoying a surprising start from the Reds, who at the time were 16–8 and riding high atop the NL Central. "There is still room for improvement in this lineup. This team could get even better," he wrote. "In the meantime, I’m having fun."You can predict some of Dotson's performance as an immigration judge through his performance in his previous professional roles. When he is given the choice between more or less punishment, he opts for more. As director of the Virginia Department of Corrections, Dotson acted on an advisory opinion written by then-Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares, who argued that the state could expand exclusions from sentence credits, beyond the written law, to prisoners who would otherwise benefit from those credits. That decision delayed the release of approximately 8,000 prisoners; Prison Legal News estimated that 560 of those prisoners had already been told that they were within a month of release. When the Virginia Supreme Court subsequently shot down Miyares's advisory opinion, Dotson's Department of Corrections delayed releasing the prisoners for another three months. A group of 53 state prisoners eventually filed a class-action lawsuit against Dotson and his predecessor, and won $1.6 million in a 2025 settlement. From the PLN article:

item.title: The Witch They Call Black Annis
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Black Annis is an English witch who supposedly ate children, which is always a good story to keep your kids from wandering in the woods at night. A written account from 300 years ago said she lived in a cave, was raised by wolves, had sharp claws, and wore a skirt made from human skin. We know the specific area the legend came from, but where is the cave? Could the story of Black Annis come from that of a 15th-century nun named Agnes who lived alone outside her convent? A woman hermit was very unusual, but Agnes seems to have been respected and even revered. However, a couple of hundred years separated those stories, and intervening events may have changed the details greatly to fit new religious narratives. There are alternate theories on the origins of the legend, and Dr. Emily Zarka goes through them to judge their accuracy.

item.title: Listen to a Long-Lost Daft Punk Mix From 1997
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: A DJ named Ralph Lawson, who hosted a radio show called Trans Europe Express, found an incredible time capsule in his collection: an hour-long mixtape sent to him by Daft Punk in 1997, shortly after the release of their debut album, Homework. The tape was badly damaged, but he worked with a specialist to restore it and has put the whole mix up on Soundcloud.As I write this, the mix has been up for a little over a day and has just over 7000 plays. It’s unclear whether Lawson ever even played it on the show, so we could be among the first people, outside of Daft Punk themselves, to hear this mix in almost 30 years.

item.title: Ohio’s Jon Husted, object of Trump’s leering, is just an empty pair of pants
item.content:encoded: Jon Husted has a problem: People can’t seem to remember who he is. The former lieutenant governor of Ohio was appointed to be the state’s junior U.S. senator in 2025, after JD Vance became vice president. But Husted hasn’t much of an impression on the Buckeye State’s residents. In an August poll conducted by Emerson College, nearly four in 10 Ohio voters answered “unsure/never heard of” when asked their opinion of the Republican incumbent. Only 14% answered the same regarding his Democratic opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown. In fact, one in four voters in a Bowling Green State University poll even mistakenly identified Brown, a popular veteran of Ohio politics, as the incumbent. (In fact, Brown lost his seat to Ohio’s other Republican senator, Bernie Moreno, in 2024.)The Husted campaign has tried to spin his forgettability as an asset, hoping to trick voters into thinking of Brown as a failed incumbent, but it doesn’t seem to be working. Brown is pulling ahead in the most recent polls, riding a larger national turn away from the GOP. So Republicans turned to the one person who knows how to get a headline: Donald Trump.Bringing the president to campaign in Ohio has certainly helped to boost Husted’s name recognition, but at a painful cost. Now Husted has become the single most famous male victim of Trump’s relentless appetite for sexual harassment. The president’s public ogling of Husted started at a Youngstown rally on Oct. 12, when Trump delivered a monologue about how he’d “started examining [Husted’s] body” and had seen big hands and shoulders. Then he said the word “ass.” This caused a reaction of shock and laughter reaction in the crowd and also generated a lot of media attention. So Trump, like a narcissistic rat pushing the “applause” button, turned it into a running joke. At nearly every rally now, whether in Ohio or somewhere else, Trump raves about the 59-year-old Husted’s reputedly spectacular and muscular backside.Trump is famously a lifelong heterosexual, so many in the media and on the left are confused. They assume that latent homoerotic yearnings are burbling up, perhaps from the disinhibition that can occur among people who take regular tests for dementia, as does our president. But that’s unlikely, and not just because Husted actually possesses the softer derrière typical of a man his age. If genuine same-sex desire was behind Trump’s leering, the overtly homophobic crowds who populate MAGA rallies would be highly uncomfortable.Bringing Trump to campaign in Ohio has certainly boost Husted’s name recognition, but at a painful cost. Now he’s the single most famous male victim of Trump’s relentless appetite for sexual harassment.Instead, as videos show, they scream with the same laughter they produce when Trump goes on a racist tirade, encourages audience members to commit acts of violence or otherwise showcases his affinity for childish bullying, which remains his main and often sole selling point to his base. It’s a large-scale version of the infamous “Access Hollywood” tape, where Trump tried to impress the show’s host, Billy Bush, with braggadocious claims that he can grab women’s genitals and they have to put up with it. The MAGA crowd may not favor the term “sexual harassment,” but they get that’s what Trump is doing to Husted. He did the same bit with Nicki Minaj, making the rapper-turned-MAGA shill stand up and show off her backside to the crowd at a Michigan rally. As feminists like to remind folks, sexual harassment is about demonstrating power, not lust. Husted is far from the only man Trump ever catcalls. As the New York Times notes, Trump loves making a spectacle out of men’s looks, for the approval of hooting MAGA audiences who get a vicarious thrill from watching Trump say inappropriate things to fellow Republicans, who have no choice but to grin and pretend they enjoy it. It’s a continuation of the other ways Trump displays his dominance over Republicans with fancy job titles, such as senators and Cabinet officials, by expecting them to flatter him grotesquely on camera or to wear ill-fitting shoes he has “gifted” them. None of this should make us feel any sympathy for Husted or other Republicans, who could at any point grow an actual spine and reject Trump’s abuse. These people grovel for their failing leader in the vain hope that some of his celebrity stardust will rub off on them and boost their political ambitions. Husted is a classic example of the problem now facing Republicans. Like most in his party, he has nothing to offer voters, unless they’re hyper-rich capitalists seeking deregulation or massive tax cuts. He has no discernible charisma of his own, either. So all that’s left is leeching onto Trump and hoping his ability to speak to the lizard-brain impulses of bigots will rally enough voters to drag Husted’s empty pair of pants (and his mediocre ass) across the finish line. Like most in his party, Husted has nothing to offer voters, unless they’re hyper-rich capitalists seeking deregulation or tax cuts, and no discernible charisma. All that’s left is leeching onto Trump and hoping his ability to speak to the lizard-brain impulses of bigots can drag Husted’s empty pants across the line.What’s funny about all this is that Husted’s blandness is likely what landed him in the unfortunate spot of getting rhetorically goosed by Trump almost every night. By his own account, Trump knew very little about the Ohio Republican he was there to support at the Youngstown rally, but learned shortly beforehand that Husted played football in college. Trump, whose background is in reality TV, resorted to his tendency to reduce a person to a single defining trait that could fit on a chyron. So even though Husted’s gridiron career ended decades ago, Trump indulged in lame fantasies about how he thinks a football player should look like, complete with broad shoulders and well-defined glutes.Likely, it would have ended with one iteration if he hadn’t praised Husted’s ass, which elevated a pedestrian effort to define a candidate into the realm of attention-getting weirdness. But of course that remark got everyone’s attention, and Trump will reliably return to any bit, no matter how bizarre, as long as it draws eyeballs. So it was that Husted, who was on the verge of being relegated to “Former College Football Player” in the sprawling reality show cast of Trump’s political orbit, instead became the butt of Trump’s favorite new joke.It could be worse, of course. Trump has a similar bit he likes to trot out about Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for that state’s Senate seat. Except instead of being an imaginary muscleman like Husted, Trump has cast Paxton in the role of ugly loser. In nearly every speech where he mentions Paxton, Trump has to talk about how hideous the guy is and how poorly he supposedly dresses.With both of these GOP candidates, Trump’s oversimplified, theatrical descriptors don’t have much to do with reality. Whatever he once looked like, Husted doesn’t really have the athletic build Trump fantasizes about. Paxton is nobody’s idea of a handsome man, but it’s simply not true that he dresses poorly. There are many terrible things we could say about Paxton, but his wardrobe appears perfectly fine — especially compared to Trump, who seems to believe that wearing enormously oversized suits will hide his ever-expanding bulk. But these two guys are now characters in Trump’s world, where, as in reality TV shows, individual humans are stripped of all their complexities to be turned into broad, easily consumed caricatures.Whether he’s inviting the world to stare at these men’s allegedly spectacular rear end or daring them to smile while he calls them ugly, Trump is sending a message: He owns these people. He can define them in reductive, humiliating language, and they have been so hollowed out as human beings that they won’t even defend themselves. Normally, when a leader is both a lame duck and cratering in his approval polls, the way Donald Trump is now, that person’s party will start looking for ways to move on and forge a new identity. It’s a sign of how empty the Republican Party is that they seem incapable of doing that. They don’t just submit to Trump’s continued abuse, but even keep seeking it out. That must be a miserable experience, but clearly they feel that without him, they’re nothing at all. It’s tough to disagree.

item.title: The real strategy of the DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit is more sinister
item.author: 1axblouew6p92pbpe56ydtxinvrtehldbz9oe7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: A new batch of data on North Carolina mail ballot rejections arrived in my inbox late Monday. Mail ballots are getting flagged for rejection at a rate of nearly 6%, as of an Oct. 24 count. That’s almost 4,000 ballots so far. When ballot counting ends, the number will likely be significantly higher.While not all ballots with problems will ultimately be thrown out, they’re in limbo and essentially null until a voter takes action to resubmit or fix errors. It’s an extra hurdle to voting that many people don’t end up surmounting. What’s more, we can now definitively tie a majority of in two of the state’s largest counties — both Democratic strongholds — to a strict new rule, imposed by Republicans at the last minute, about sealing the inner envelope.If that wasn’t enough, the latest data revealed striking rejection rates in the double digits for some of North Carolina’s most rural counties where Black voters comprise a majority of the population. Those with lower internet access and fewer resources may have never gotten the memo that there’s an entirely new and arbitrary rule about ballot sealing. And now, it could cost them their vote.

item.title: At noon today, DOJ must reveal which states it pressured
item.author: 1axbwuejwrskfhlcmsabky17r6fy3l75ojcnab@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Among DOJ’s objections was that the request covered communications from July 1 to the present. DOJ wanted to limit it to the last 30 days. That would have hidden what the agencies did in July, August and September.The question is why. What are they hiding? What threats have they made? What deals have they cut?I am not naive enough to think that one court order requiring an answer to one question will end Trump’s assault on free and fair elections. I know that even after this disclosure, much of this pressure campaign will remain secret.But it is an important step toward understanding the scope and scale of this scheme to corrupt the midterm vote count.Interestingly, in his order, Judge Boasberg offered DOJ and DHS a way out of answering this question, and out of the entire lawsuit. “Defendants may moot this process at any time,” he wrote, “by filing a notice indicating that they will not engage in the conduct sought to be enjoined in connection with the upcoming election.”In other words, if Trump and his cronies simply agree to stop threatening and coercing election officials and workers into not counting votes, the entire case will go away. Yet they will never accept this simple resolution.Trump wants the threats to continue. Indeed, he wants them to escalate. And they are escalating.According to The New York Times, DOJ has now served grand jury subpoenas on election workers in Los Angeles County, ordering them to appear with records on Nov. 4, the day after the election.The next step could well be search warrants and threats of indictment.We are in the midst of a constitutional crisis in which the federal government has weaponized itself against free and fair elections. It is using its vast array of tools and hiding the full extent of its actions from public view.We will have many more fights in the days and weeks ahead. I have no illusions about how hard this will be. A weaponized federal government is a dangerous adversary.But at noon today, at least part of that veil of secrecy will lift. We will learn which states DOJ and DHS have been pressuring in the dark, and I will share what we learn as soon as we can.We have to stand tall and fight back.

item.title: Sakura Tsuruta
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Sakura Tsuruta, a Japanese electronic musician from Tokyo. She studied classical piano growing up, and became interested in the therapeutic application of music in high school when her grandfather faced dementia. At Berklee College of Music she studied music therapy and electronic production; she thereafter worked at a hospice, using music in palliative care. That experience led her to start making music herself, in which she fuses her classical background and electronic production techniques. We’re starting with her 2024 LP, , a collection of eight tracks that combine driving bass lines, precise percussion, and melodic arpeggios and leads. We’re also playing her 2022 LP,

This is a relatively new entrant into the election modeling/forecasting world. They’re a bit more cautious than Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin, seeing the most likely outcome as Democrats taking 52 seats versus 53. That’s probably actually technically the median result of running numerous modeling simulations. In any case, I was looking at the categories in which they place different races. For instance, they put Texas, as “Lean D”, so more likely to flip than Ohio, Maine and Iowa. I’m not sure that’s wrong. But it’s just wild to see.
