item.title: Rest In Peace, Patrick Stewart (1940-2026)
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: He was largely considered an unknown when the “Star Trek” offer came along. At the invitation of a friend, a university professor, Mr. Stewart had been in Los Angeles conducting master classes on Shakespeare when, one evening, he gave a lecture and performed some bits of the plays in a program that was open to the public. A TV producer who was involved in developing a new “Star Trek” series happened to attend and soon persuaded Mr. Stewart to audition — even though, as Mr. Stewart later wrote, he knew “next to nothing” about the franchise.Surprised to get the part — the “Star Trek” creator, Gene Roddenberry, who was overseeing the new series, had not been keen to hire him at first — Mr. Stewart expected the project to be a short-term commitment. How, he remembered thinking, could the show possibly succeed with a middle-aged pacifist captain with a French name and a British accent?This is hard news to take, even though Stewart lived a full and fulfilling life. The Next Generation will always be my favorite Star Trek series and Picard my favorite captain. Stewart got off to a rough start on the series:So when he was on set shooting the show’s debut season and co-stars like Jonathan Frakes, Denise Crosby and Brent Spiner would tease him or ad-lib a joke or laugh when they flubbed their lines, it would low-key infuriate him.“I could be a severe bastard,” he writes. “My experiences at the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre had been intense and serious… On the TNG set, I grew angry with the conduct of my peers, and that’s when I called that meeting in which I lectured the cast for goofing off and responded to Denise Crosby’s, ‘We’ve got to have some fun sometimes, Patrick’ comment by saying, ‘We are not here, Denise, to have fun.’”“In retrospect,” Stewart continues, “everyone, me included, finds this story hilarious. But in the moment, when the cast erupted in hysterics at my pompous declaration, I didn’t handle it well. I didn’t enjoy being laughed at. I stormed off the set and into my trailer, slamming the door.”Q: There’s a passage where you say that, from your father, “I drew Picard’s stern, intimidating tendencies. But I like to think that my mother is in the captain too, in his moments of warmth and sensitivity.” Do you see Picard as your way of reconciling that conflict between your parents?A: Very much so, yes. Both Star Trek and therapy have been responsible for that. Having to open the doors into my childhood in order to be an actor became utterly intriguing to me in a way that it never had been before. And I regret that when I look back on some of the roles I played, what I might have brought to them if I just released myself a little bit more.

item.title: Second to none
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: One Wisconsin man, waiting for a flight to Milwaukee, stood and gazed at the sign two gates away: Tampa. Another, splayed on the airport carpet, trying to wrangle his restless kids with an iPad showing the Packers game, said he had just come from there, had tried to rearrange his family’s schedule to stay for two, three more days. Because the Brewers, by then up 2-0 in the World Series, were on their way.This was in Nashville, Sunday afternoon. My wife and I were sitting at the gate in between, headed back to New York. All weekend, we had marveled at the preponderance of Brewers fans traipsing around town in jerseys, T-shirts, hats, talking about ticket prices and family members who ponied up, who skipped planned vacations to watch the franchise’s first World Series championship. In a city 564 miles from Milwaukee, everyone with any connection to Wisconsin was making sure to show it. And 725 miles from Tropicana Field, almost halfway there, they were thinking about Tampa, glancing toward it, itching to be there for their heroes’ increasingly imminent, some might say inevitable, coronation.When the moment arrived Wednesday night — the Brewers taking the game and the series over the Rays, 4-1 — thousands of fans in blue and yellow injected the road ballpark with the rapture of home. Thousands more were at American Family Field to jubilate together. The enthusiasm, the reach, of major-league baseball’s smallest city felt huge.The Brewers’ title was not sudden, not a surprise. It rode atop a swell of success that has been building since 2016, under David Stearns’ front office and then roaring on through Matt Arnold’s promotion from within. Eight postseason appearances, six division crowns, three NLCS appearances. An MVP, a Cy Young and another in the offing. Pride was there, with plenty of reason for it. But it was closely held, a targeted fire hose rather than a crashing wave, until this week.The impulse, mine and yours and the masses’, is to explain a newly observed phenomenon, to track that wave back to its origin. Their Triple-A affiliate is in Nashville, could that be … no the tie only dates to 2020. Were the Packers in town facing the Titans? Nope. Is this America’s team for dethroning the Dodgers? Are the 2026 Brewers the protagonists of a soaring sequel to Moneyball? Are they a blueprint being copied as they are celebrated?Is this how any team would feel on the cusp of its first championship? Is this what it looks like when the search for an explanation widens beyond logic, beyond words, and opens up into something that can only be described as an experience?The day it was agreed to back in December 2022, a three-way trade between the Braves, A’s and Brewers was called the Sean Murphy deal. The offshoot of the trade that redirected catcher William Contreras to the Brewers for speedster Esteury Ruiz was a noteworthy but secondary concern.History has perspective that headlines don’t. Last night, as Contreras hit, challenged and implored his way to World Series MVP honors, the Brewers forced the baseball world to look at them from a new angle. Because of money or media concentration or the happenstance of postseason results, the club with the most wins over the past three seasons has not been held in the regard that record would imply.Their championship and vengeful sweep of the Dodgers barrels the sport out of a particular type of tunnel vision. For years and years, as the postseason field expanded, “it was easy to see the playoffs as a crapshoot,” Matthew Trueblood wrote recently.“Then, Shohei Ohtani signed with the Dodgers and won it all twice in a row, and it was like the God particle had been discovered all over again,” Trueblood said. “That messy egalitarianism that seemed to have settled over the sport burned off like low-lying fog on an unseasonably warm autumn morning, and we all saw (or imagined, at least) the ugly truth: Only power matters; only money wins.”There was a time, not three years ago, when the Dodgers’ long run of excellence was still unvested. They were the best team in baseball, but that was valued on paper rather than in gold.Overnight, the Brewers have called for a new assessment. The season they just completed — 103 wins, with an 11-2 playoff mission completed against the best competition available — was second to none. In degree of dominance and difficulty, it compares favorably to every champ since the 2018 Red Sox. They are two regular season wins clear of the Dodgers in the very years of the supposed Ohtani dynasty, they have a World Series pennant headed to the rafters, a young team and booming farm system in tow.Is this Brewers team an underdog story with a happy ending or an adamant arrival of something else entirely?How, exactly, did you grow up? How did you fall in love? How did you get to where you are today? Do you really know? Was there a discrete, usable process involved? Or do you, in the grand tradition of the major religions, recount a singular story with the conviction of universal truth?The Brewers’ motto was everywhere in October: . But it’s a mantra, not an invitation. Milwaukee’s way lends itself to uncertainty. Under Stearns and Arnold, they have sustained winning teams on a middling ownership-imposed budgets by trading away a number of established stars (Corbin Burnes, Josh Hader, Devin Williams, Freddy Peralta) in favor of starter packs full of young, promising, unknown commodities. They fill out rosters by sifting for high-potential waiver claims and unheralded trade chips, not winning free agent bidding wars.In 2026, they wound up with three of the 30 most valuable players in baseball, and those players were 24 (Jacob Misiorowski), 26 (Brice Turang) and 22 (Jackson Chourio). Turang’s breakout last year was the only 4-WAR season among the group entering the spring. Two more 3-WAR hitters (Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell) had never even amassed 500 plate appearances in a single major-league season. The starting shortstop who batted .354 in the postseason (Cooper Pratt) had not yet glimpsed Triple-A.They gave rookie pitchers 80 starts, more than any other team in the sport. The oldest and least acclaimed of those arms, Robert Gasser, finished with the most starts and registered the best starting pitching performance of the World Series.Uncertainty, in such regular doses, is hard to distinguish from skepticism when viewed through a quantified lens.Over this decade-long ascent, the Brewers have persistently outfoxed wise and grounded projection systems. First, they did it under the professorial watch of Stearns and Craig Counsell. When Counsell took a larger contract for the rival Cubs, Arnold promoted Pat Murphy, grizzled motivator of men, the most football coach of baseball manager. He delights in the undershot projections, feeding them to his team like fuel to a fire.So many of them had felt like they were second-best, the second choice. And the ones who hadn’t? Well, Murphy made sure they would, as part of the collective unit that was less proven than the Dodgers, less appealing than the Cubs, less respected than they had earned.Projecting the Brewers to do all the things they did would have been malpractice. Not projecting all those things turned out to be wrong. Would you believe it if you didn’t see it?Belief is necessary. It’s the quotidian forward force, the gas in the combustion engine that carries you to work and the grocery store and back home again. Seeing, with thousands of others who waited and believed alongside you on the same warm nights, sitting in the same traffic, that’s transcendent. It’s the wind in your hair at sunset, driving 75 on a wide open highway. It's the thing you get up and start each day to reach.Throngs of Brewers fans took over Tropicana Field to see something bigger and less nebulous than overachievement. Like the outfield fences, the walls of collective understanding are arbitrarily drawn. Winning the World Series isn’t necessarily harder than winning 103 games or winning the division every year, but getting over that wall means something different. It’s a license for collective joy.It gets Christian Yelich jerseys packed in suitcases and Chourio jerseys purchased a size bigger than the kids need right now. It gets plane tickets booked and tattoos designed. It moves broadcasters and Cy Young winners to tears.No explanation is needed. ⚾️Jacob Misiorowski has found a perfect match. The woman who gave the broadcast a fantastic GIF-able facial expression …In addition to being the most football coach of baseball managers, Pat Murphy is the obvious choice for a hypothetical Reporters’ Favorite award.He even threw in an intentional mispronunciation of social media quip, which has a 100% chance of being quoted. “I’m not on social media, Twizzler or Instacart, whatever,” the AP has Murphy saying.I’m not accusing anyone of bias. I’m just noting the reality that Murphy is both constitutionally and topically perfect for the baseball media.Contreras’ older brother Willson, who has been openly affected by the hardship in their native country, was on hand wearing his brother’s jersey and tearfully celebrating with him on the field afterward.Joe Davis, the lead FOX play-by-play announcer, specializes in echos of baseball broadcasts past.When the Rays eventually came back to win in 12, he joined the linage of his predecessor, Joe Buck (who was adapting his own father’s call), when he yelled, “We’ll see you later tonight,” over the post-midnight walk-off knock.Davis’ flair for the cleverly deployed reference sometimes overshadows his original work, which tends toward the strong but subtle. But this is another area where time will crystallize the potency of the work. Last year, he punctuated the Dodgers’ epic Game 7 win with one I could see sticking for the ages: “To beat the champ, you gotta knock ‘em out.”“Unshakeable, unstoppable, and champions at last: The Milwaukee Brewers.”The part where I ask for your supportThis is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

item.title: Atlanta Took Golden State’s Lunch Money
item.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
item.content:encoded: Five games into the Finals, it felt odd that we’d yet to watch the game where one team makes everything. The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries do both take great pride in their defenses, and their offenses do each have certain limitations. Golden State’s heavy diet of threes, for instance, leaves them prone to variance. But that means, you know, that the shooting numbers should vary—not be resolutely bad for two weeks.After Game 2, when the sludge of Game 1 appeared to carry over and the Dream tied the series, a reporter asked Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase why she thought it had been such a struggle for these teams to score. Nakase didn’t take the question too seriously. “What’s our identity?” she said, panning the room, the impatient teacher in front of her class. “What? You guys should know this.”Two of the league’s top defenses, sure. Even so, the numbers were bad. The reporter pressed Nakase again.

item.title: Star Wars: The Radio Drama
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Somehow I’d never heard of this before: NPR produced and aired radio dramatizations of the films in the original Star Wars trilogy. The first program was particularly popular, garnering NPR hundreds of thousands of new listeners. The original versions are available in full on The Internet Archive:All three programs contain elements of John Williams’ original soundtrack. Mark Hamill and Anthony Daniels reprised their movie roles for the first two radio programs and some other bold-faced names made appearances throughout: Billy Dee Williams as Lando Calrissian, John Lithgow as Yoda (??), Ed Begley Jr. as Boba Fett (???), David Alan Grier as a nameless X-wing fighter pilot, and Nia Vardalos.The radio programs were based on the original film scripts with some added scenes; from Open Culture:With science-fiction novelist Brian Daley brought on to add or restore scenes to the script of the original dialogue-light feature film, the story stretches out to thirteen episodes for a total runtime of six hours. The series thus stands as an early example of the expansion of the Star Wars universe that, in all kinds of media, has continued apace ever since.Daley adapted the script partly using material from earlier drafts of Lucas’s scripts, and restored several scenes cut from the final edit of the film, as well as adding original new scenes created specially for the audio version. The narrative of the first two episodes takes place entirely before the opening scene of the 1977 film, and expands the background to events leading up to the capture of the Tantive IV spacecraft above the planet Tatooine. Episode 1, largely based on cut scenes from the original, explores the life of Luke Skywalker on Tatooine. During the story, Luke’s skyhopper (a vehicle seen in the background in Luke’s garage during the film) is damaged during a desert race; Luke sees the distant Star Destroyer battle in the sky; and he is reunited with his childhood friend, Biggs Darklighter. Episode 2, made up of material written entirely by Daley, provides backstory to Princess Leia’s acquisition of the Death Star plans from agents of the Rebel Alliance on the planet Toprawa. In scenes set on the planet Alderaan, Leia discusses the plans with her father, Prestor Organa, and determines to go in search of Obi-Wan Kenobi.These versions, boldly called The Definitive Editions (Hope, Empire, Jedi), include opening scrolls and images taken from Star Wars comic books and trading cards:Yes, that’s a script turned into a movie turned into an audio drama turned into a, uh, quasi-cinematic Powerpoint? (via open culture)

item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over atIn case you missed it a week ago, The Athletic published this extremely detailedreport from Jourdan Rodrigue and Mike Sando on how NFL game-day communications work. I encourage you to read the entire thing in full, because it includes a lot of sweet tea, including stories about head coaches angrily firing their assistants over the headset (then changing their minds the next day) and, dearer to my heart, one assistant coach staying on the channel while he had to take a frantic piss. My kindred spirit.As with all things NFL, these communication systems are coordinated with near-military fuss. The graphic design in the story includes multiple ornate diagrams that outline how all of this shit works. We see how dozens of coaches on the sideline are talking with one another, on the field and up in the booth, during a game. We also see all of the tech crew workers behind the bench, wearing different-colored hats to signify which of them are in charge of keeping the radio channels private, which ones service the Microsoft tablets that players love to angrily smash on the ground, and such and such. All of these people are connected by a series of invisible lines so tangled, it looks like an old-timey phone switchboard when laid out on paper.

item.title: The election chaos is about to play out in three scary phases.
item.author: delivery_20261029100502.48141097.4768@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
The midterm elections are now underway across the country and as voters decide who should hold the levers of power in Washington, all eyes are on President Donald Trump. He’s spent the last decade baselessly questioning the integrity of U.S. elections—despite plenty of evidence finding they are safe and secure—with things coming to a violent head on Jan. 6, 2021. This year, as more and more polling is suggesting Democrats will sweep Republicans, even in solidly red districts, it raises the question: Will the president accept the results of critical House and Senate races, or won’t he? “I will, if they’re honest elections,” Trump ominously responded when asked this very question on Tuesday.
Since Trump began his second term, he’s been laying the groundwork to try to nationalize U.S. elections and go after “voter fraud” through executive action and lawsuits against states, though most of these efforts have been struck down in court. Yet, the Justice Department has not given up. In fact, in recent weeks the agency filed at least two more dubious election lawsuits against California and Alaska, plus a series of cases against immigrants for alleged noncitizen voting. The legal challenges suggest the administration is planning ahead this time around, planting lawsuits that might create a foothold in the courts for the GOP to seize on if the midterms don’t end up going their way.
To Charles Stewart III, a political scientist and professor at MIT who has spent decades studying American congressional politics, elections, and political development, the current situation created by Trump is a test of America’s democracy. “Not primarily because of fundamental shortcomings in American election administration, but because political actors associated with the Administration will attempt to delegitimize or overturn its work,” he wrote in a newly published paper, “The Day After: Threats and Guardrails in the 2026 Election.”
Stewart believes that Trump’s efforts to thwart this year’s midterms should be viewed in three distinct phases: Before Election Day, during the vote counting and certification process, and when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. In practice, this looks like Trump beginning to seed baseless claims that losing Republicans can make after Election Day: mail ballots are suspect, voter rolls are contaminated with noncitizens, slow ballot counts are evidence of fraud, and any Democratic victories in close races shouldn’t be accepted. After Election Day, the lawsuits begin, harkening back to the days and weeks following Trump’s 2020 loss to Joe Biden, and finally things might culminate at the Capitol, where lawmakers could be pressured not to certify election winners. I spoke with Stewart to understand how this framework can help us see important red flags in the hours immediately following Election Day, plus the chances that Trump incites yet another angry mob to take over the Capitol. And is there silver lining to hold on to? Here’s our conversation, lightly edited and condensed for clarity.Shirin Ali: In your paper, you drill down on the president’s efforts to undermine the midterms into three flashpoints: Before Election Day, during the vote counting and certification process, and when the new Congress convenes. Can you explain what each of these are? The ideas behind those flashpoints come from what we've seen the Trump administration working on in the second term: two executive orders, activities at the Justice Department and Homeland Security, actions that are beginning to nibble around the edges of the election administration process. Particularly before Election Day, putting pressures on mail voting, highlighted by the executive order from this past March that basically directed the U.S. Postal Service to create a new series of procedures for handling mail voting, marrying that together with directives to DHS to create these lists of citizens.
The second flashpoint has to do with pressures on election administration, especially election administrators and the institutions themselves. There, I think the pressures go beyond even what the administration has been doing. Certainly, a lot of the activity of the administration has been focused on the possibility that if election officials don't do what the administration wants, they will not only bring civil complaints against them, but they may very well bring criminal complaints against them. Then after Election Day, that's where we're thinking about getting the final count in. We shift into the formal process of canvassing the vote, certifying it, and making sure that we've named the winners. I'm thinking broadly about a potential replay of what happened after the 2020 election, where the Trump campaign lodged a number of lawsuits in battleground states like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. I'm still anticipating, even more now, that coming true.
The final flashpoint is what happens when the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027, particularly the House. And there the question is whether there will be efforts to bar the seating of senators or members of the House who've been elected, specifically Democrats who would be the pivotal members of the two chambers that would flip control of the chamber to the Democrats. There's another obvious parallel with 2020, when there were efforts to deny the certification of the presidential election. How do the Justice Department’s lawsuits against California and Alaska fit into this? Those are kind of jumping the gun on the timeline that I had suspected, because they're really almost preempting post-election challenges and making them pre-election challenges. About a week ago I was saying, “Well, they've filed this lawsuit against California, it’s getting kind of close to the election. If there's just California, it's kind of a weak rule in terms of applying formal pressure on the states.” Then came Alaska, and this one makes me wonder what else the DOJ is going to do in the next week to bring early lawsuits against states and kind of do a shot across the bow.
The California lawsuit is the sort of thing that we that we've long expected the Trump administration to do, and in fact in the first administration, there were rumors that they were trying to put together a national voter database and merge it with immigration records to begin to go after states for having noncitizens on the rolls. This has been a long dream of the administration and people associated with the administration, and it's taken them basically a decade in order to act on it. It doesn't look like they've done a particularly sophisticated job, both in terms of the actual job of database matching or on the legal side.
The Alaska case seems to be the most frivolous election challenge that I can imagine, and in fact it's kind of orthogonal. It's unrelated to the things I had anticipated, because the lawsuit they're bringing is the sort of lawsuit that you would expect a candidate to bring. Really, it's up to Sen. Sullivan to bring these challenges under Alaska law and then potentially to bring a contest to the U.S. Senate. I only have to believe that the Alaska case is the classic case of pleasing an audience of one; Donald Trump wanted it and he got it. There's just no way in the world this is going to go forward. It's sort of like going after James Comey or going after the members of Congress who reminded service members they didn't have to follow illegal orders. It's really performative, to please the boss, and hard to take seriously, except the degree to which it's predictive of what we're likely to see after the election: the federal government putting the thumb on the scales of candidate-oriented post-election litigation. Next week, immediately after Election Day is over, what are you going to be watching for? I think there will be two things. One will be legitimate, and the other will be illegitimate. The legitimate thing is that we may very well see more losing candidates contest their elections and begin taking legal actions to try to save evidence, within the normal contest laws. Some of it may very well be performative to garner support from the administration or local political actors, but those are the ill-fated sorts of things that there's a legal framework for doing. Plus there's a legal framework for judges throwing these cases out, right? And that's the way it should happen.
What I think we need to be prepared for, and I don't think it's going to be widespread, are candidates supported by the administration going into court to attempt to impound voting machines and ballots and to remove them from where they're normally housed. Basically, a repeat of the Fulton County event a year ago where the FBI removed ballots. Those are the things I think we should anticipate, and I think that the Department of Justice may very well take matters into their own hands that are quasi-independent of the candidates themselves. For instance, the Alaska lawsuit was just something that the DOJ did because the president wanted it. That’s a disturbing thing that I think we need to be prepared for after the election because we've already seen it happen before the election. That is the DOJ just going into places they don't like and filing lawsuits. In your paper, you wrote, “The greatest danger is not that even a few challenges will succeed; it is that a small number of delayed certifications could matter greatly if control of either chamber is in doubt.” What did you mean by that? If you think about Jan. 6, 2021, in Congress and leading up to that, there was a whole lot of noise in the political system about whether the vice president could refuse to accept electors and whether Congress could impose their own view on what state electors they should accept, and all those sorts of things. In retrospect, traditional constitutional election lawyers had it right all along in terms of the law. The correct person was elected president, but the political ramifications of that whole episode and Jan. 6 itself were just catastrophic for American politics and certainly transformative in many ways. The law held, the right guy was elected president, but antidemocratic elements were energized and we had a riot at the Capitol.
A social movement has arisen in the country that makes millions of dollars based on stoking a view that elections in America are illegitimate. It's an extreme view, and a minority view even within the Republican Party at that level of extremity, but it's really been politically consequential over the last six years. I think we could be in an Act 2 of that, and that's what I'm getting at here. Imagine that this was a decade ago and we're coming into a Congress where the Democrats were going to take over the chamber and have about a 20-seat lead. You wouldn't have imagined anything major to come out of any contest, any seat. There might have been a couple of contests and it might have been highly politicized, but they would have been handled in the regular order.
Imagine right now if Democrats have that same margin of success. I think we have to assume there will be at least a few members of the House on the Republican side who will make a lot of hay around refusing their being seated, refusing to allow them to vote for the speaker, pressuring the clerk not to accept their certificates of election, those sorts of things. All of those would be illegitimate. The rules of the House are very clear about the clerk of the House accepting the properly given certificates of election for members of the House for the purpose of the roll-call vote at the beginning and electing the speaker. There is a very prescribed way of handling contests in the House of Representatives, and there is no legitimate, legal way for the current Congress to be the judge of those elections.
Now, one of the things I think will stoke the political fires, though, is the investigations into any contest that any member would want to bring in the 119th Congress. There will be pressures in the current Congress for House Speaker Mike Johnson to highly politicize those investigations, use them as opportunities to shine a spotlight on California and other states that are not cooperating with the administration over noncitizens on the rolls, for instance. Or on states with high levels of mail voting. It's going to unleash this political theater in hopes of blowing up regular procedures that are very clear, much more clear than the Electoral Count Act was in 2020, into something that looks like a rejection of this election. And the closer it is, the higher the stakes and the higher the temperature. Despite having serious concerns about what the Trump administration will do in the event Republicans lose control of Congress, you’re optimistic that the 2026 midterms will be resilient enough to withstand a Trump bashing. Why? It starts with the decentralized nature of election administration. When I've been asked about whether the Trump administration is going to be successful in overthrowing this election, I've generally responded with two words: —they've not been very good at what they've done; and there are just not enough lawyers left in the Department of Justice, or enough immigration agents, there's not enough of anything to take over the American electoral system. If it's a matter of mobilizing the federal government, there are more local election officials running elections than there's the capacity of the Trump administration to go after enough of them. That’s decentralization.
The second thing is that we continue to see evidence that the facts-based institutions of our electoral system continue to hold. That includes state and local election officials who are nothing if not careful about following the law. And there are the county boards of elections; we've seen general election boards stand by the canvassed results. There have been several states that have passed laws over the last few years reinforcing the notion that the certifications of elections at the local level are ministerial and that the proper place for conducting contests, if something is seen to be amiss, is in the court system, not in the election boards. Finally, I think we continue to see the courts holding to what the law is, holding to the precedents that have been established in the past about what do you do when someone contests the results of an election. There's established law there, and trial courts have, on the whole, held, and when they haven't, they've been admonished or overturned on appeal. It would be nice if we didn't have to say, “Well, at the end of the day, we're relying on the Alaska Supreme Court.” It would be much better if it didn't have to get that far, but we do still have a robust and independent judiciary that has been willing to stand up to nonsense.

item.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

item.title: Skye Blakely Ushers In The Next Era Of USA Gymnastics With Gold
item.author: Diana Moskovitz
item.content:encoded: My favorite moment from this year's World Gymnastics Championships was the second after Skye Blakely hit the final pose in her floor routine. For a second, she was all smiles, sass, and confidence, radiating exactly the energy her sport's judges want to see. Then the music ended, Blakely's muscles released, and the 21-year-old from Texas looked like she might cry. The performance was done and Blakely could once again be exactly who she was: a young woman who had just done something very difficult.That routine capped Blakely's first all-around gold medal, which was one of four medals Blakely brought home this week from the Netherlands—her gold joined a Team USA silver, as well as individual bronzes for herself on uneven bars and vault. A pair of Americans—Claire Pease and Reese Esponda—took individual gold and silver on the floor, respectively, in Rotterdam, while Pease also won silver on vault. On the men's side, Fred Richard won gold on the men's floor, making him the country's first gold medalist on that exercise since Paul Hamm in 2003.In other words, even if Simone Biles doesn't come back for the 2028 Olympic Games, women's gymnastics seems to be in good shape. In fact, Blakely's win meant the United States went a whopping without being home to the reigning women's all-around champion, as Biles had previously won the title in 2023 (at Worlds) and 2024 (the Paris Olympics). Even that requires an asterisk because at last year's Worlds, American Leanne Wong took home the all-around silver.

item.title: Don’t Follow the Early Vote! Except For This
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I jest, a bit, in the title. As I’ve told you several times, friends don’t let friends watch the early vote. But there’s one thing I want to point your attention to. I’ll explain in a moment why this leaves me mainly consistent. There’s one thing that seems to be showing up fairly consistently across the country and particularly in the Deep South. That is a high proportion of generally younger, non-regular Democratic voters. And they tend to be less white, relative to the rest of the electorate. In a number of Deep South states you’re seeing high turnout for non-regular Democratic voters which in states like Mississippi for instance means mostly Black voters.

item.title: Trump Is on an Absurd Collision Course With Yet Another Federal Judge
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Trump DOJ’s No. 3 Official in the Hot SeatA golf course in D.C. is the improbable venue for another significant Trump II showdown between the executive and judicial branches.Unlike, say, the Alien Enemies Act, Abrego Garcia, and immigrant habeas cases, where the actions that precipitated the conflict between the Trump administration and federal judges were unmistakably serious deprivations of liberty, the East Potomac Golf Course case has layers of absurdism, which we’ll get into below.My main reason for catching you up on this second-tier constitutional confrontation is to preview an important hearing in the case tomorrow, so that I can come back to this later without burdening you with a whole bunch of backstory.U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had already ordered the Trump DOJ to show cause by yesterday why it should not be ordered to preserve all records in the case in what could only be interpreted as a prelude to her considering sanctions against government lawyers for allegedly misleading her. Reyes was particularly focused on the Trump DOJ’s failure to comply with her orders to provide sufficient notice of the surprise removal of hundreds of trees on the golf course over the Columbus Day weekend.But now Judge Reyes has a new bone to pick with the Trump DOJ.Judge Reyes has suspected that the mass tree removal over the holiday weekend was part of Trump’s plan to remake the historic golf course without congressional approval — but the administration and DOJ lawyers have denied it, repeatedly and emphatically.Then on Tuesday, on her own, Judge Reyes took judicial notice of a new Truth Social post by President Trump, in which he declared that the golf course will be closing on Nov. 15, and demanded to know why the Trump DOJ had previously told her otherwise:Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told the Court on October 19 that “[w]ith regard to the November 15th date… there is no plan to close the course.” The Court ORDERS Defendants to clarify, as part of their response to the Court’s show-cause order from October 26, whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026. And, if so, how that can be reconciled with Associate AG Woodward’s representation to the Court.In her order, Reyes also scheduled a “status hearing” for Friday and ordered Woodward — who represented Trump’s co-defendants in the Mar-a-Lago case and Jan. 6 rioters — to appear at the hearing in person. The DOJ’s No. 3 personally handling cases is unheard of, let alone doing the president’s dirty work. Getting hauled into court for allegedly misleading a judge is beyond next level stuff.Yesterday, in his response to the court order, Woodward conceded that there is a plan to close the golf course, but he did not reconcile his prior statements to the contrary:The undersigned acknowledges the President has twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15. Accordingly, Interior, acting through counsel, is working to develop a plan to implement that direction and will provide this Court with notice pursuant to the Court’s October 26, 2026, Order.That prompted another stern order from Judge Reyes ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, which she has now recast as a show cause hearing that is quite a bit broader than merely whether the Trump DOJ must preserve documents in the case:The Court ORDERS the Government to come prepared to state at the hearing: (1) whether it continues to maintain that there is no final agency action; (2) the dates and times at which President Trump “twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15”; … and (3) the first date “Interior, acting through counsel” began “working to develop a plan to implement that direction,” id. Associate Attorney General Woodward remains ORDERED to appear at the hearing in person. The Court FURTHER ORDERS the attendance of at least one counsel from the Department of the Interior’s Office of the Solicitor with pre-existing experience on this case.Shortly thereafter, Woodward provided the court-required detailed notice of the administration’s plan to shut down the vast majority of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, even though the renovation plan at issue will not have been approved yet on the administration’s own timetable.The ostensible reason for closing the golf course before getting approval for the renovation is familiar: “significant safety hazards.” It’s similar to the pretext offered for the separate closure of the Kennedy Center, another D.C. public asset that Trump has tried to turn into a personal project. In this case, the public safety hazard is an allegedly “deteriorated sea wall that is currently crumbling into the Potomac River.”All of this is to tee up tomorrow’s show cause hearing for you. It’s admittedly an odd sideshow in the last week before Election Day. But it wouldn’t be Trump lawlessness without a heaping dose of absurdity.Trump DOJ Election Interference Watch: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter late yesterday rejected the Trump DOJ’s request to force Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters. In a stirring opinion, Judge Carter repeatedly blasted the Trump administration’s interference in California’s election:Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch. In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.: The Trump DOJ seized on a NYT investigation that tied the campaign of Mary Peltola to a scheme to add a second Dan Sullivan to the ballot. In a new filing by DOJ No. 3 official Stan Woodward, he withdrew his prior opposition to the Peltola campaign and the DSCC intervening in the DOJ lawsuit to block certification of the Senate election. Instead, Woodward said DOJ would use expedited discovery in the case to investigate the alleged “sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up a sham candidate for the purpose of deceiving Alaskan voters” and whether the Peltola campaign “attempted to deceive” the court. UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen assesses the legal implications of this whole mess.: Secretary of State Steve Hobbs told the Trump DOJ that its purported list of 400 alleged noncitizen voters contained actual U.S. citizens. In a letter, Hobbs said it would “irresponsible and illegal” to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from voters on the Trump DOJ list.SPLC Reveals Its Theory of the Case Against ItThe Southern Poverty Law Center has revealed in a new filing its theory of how the vindictive prosecution of it by the Trump administration came to be.The civil rights group alleges that the Trump DOJ — which has zeroed in on the SPLC’s former program of using white supremacists as paid informants against other white supremacists — was able to flip the SPLC’s own longest-tenured informant into a government informant against the SPLC because he had failed to pay income taxes for 30 years.The SPLC alleges that the flipped informant practically became a member of the prosecution team, with numerous meetings and 1,800 text messages between him and investigators over the last year. Identified in the filing as “F-9,” the informant also provided documents, reports, and four so-called “Intelligence Briefings” to investigators, the SPLC alleges:To be clear, F-9 should have been merely a in this case. But the government has treated him like part of the prosecutorial team itself, choosing to allow F-9 to decide which of the documents, recordings, and photographs in his possession he will produce, and how and when he will produce them. F-9 admitted that he has a “house full of documents,” some of which he has referenced plans to “shred.”The immediate purpose of the SPLC’s new filing was to obtain permission to subpoena the informant and obtain a court order for the informant to preserve the materials in his possession.Quote of the Day: Transformers Edition“The Arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats. It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense.”—

item.title: The Rays Never Played A Home Game In The World Series
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The Tampa Bay Rays have been dogged in their pursuit of excellence without extravagance, a process that is now two decades along and which has been hugely successful, provided your wall calendar is missing the months of October and November. They have mastered the technique of buying low, selling at an advantageous price, then rebuilding by buying low again so fully that they have convinced many of the league's other owners that theirs is the one true path. They have beaten baseball's mythical salary cap by staying below whatever it would be through simple discipline—as in, refusal to pay market-rate big-league salaries—and industry-leading player development. Good for them; they win a lot of ballgames most summers, and the owners meeting every winter. The ring for that must be enormous.But the Rays received a harsh education in this World Series, and not merely by being eradicated in five games by the Milwaukee Brewers. Other than the 12th inning of Game 4, the Rays left no footprint on the series; in every inning played before midnight in the Eastern Time Zone, they were the inferior team. They were overwhelmed by the Brewers' superior bullpen, the off-brand heroism of Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, and the more predictable heroism of William Contreras and Jackson Chourio. The difference between the best team in baseball and the best team in the American League was exactly as advertised.That's not the problem the Rays face today, though. There is little shame in losing as they did, because the Brewers were the better team when the series began as well as when it ended. Someone finishes second every year. We know this. We checked.

item.title: The Remarkable Serbian Election
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I’ve been reading a bit about the recent election in Serbia and some of the details are fascinating. A student-led coalition toppled the 12-year corrupt reign of “the increasingly authoritarian leader” Aleksandar Vučić in recent elections. But in order to ensure voters and allies that this wasn’t a grab for power on the part of the students, the students ruled themselves out.Supporters had the votes, but they needed the losing side to stay. The strict rules were a promise: to those who had opposed running, that it would not turn the movement into a party; to voters, that the list was no party in disguise.No student may run: anyone enrolled in 2024/25, or with studies on hold, is excluded. The drafters wanted no suggestion that students were building political careers. Former members of the ruling coalition’s 20 parties are barred, and so are former officials of parliamentary opposition parties. That leaves doctors, academics, artists, former athletes and activists. Ordinary members of opposition parties were not barred, but almost none with a party past. The list is led by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and professor in Novi Sad.The students’ list of 250 candidates is remarkable in itself. Comprising professors, scientists, doctors, workers, actors and activists, the candidates — most of whom had been unknown to the public — were selected through a lengthy sequence of scrutiny and interviews. University faculties proposed candidates, then reviewed nominees from across the country. After discussing the options, student assemblies made their choices. Thousands participated in this decision-making process — an extraordinary experiment in bringing direct democracy into mainstream politics.The established opposition, meanwhile, has been pushed aside, with many of its parties backing the student list. The student movement has turned the election into something like a referendum on the regime, captured in its slogan: “Serbia or the mafia.” Many assumed the students were too inexperienced or naïve for electoral politics. But with some polls putting support for the student list above 40 percent, the race appears to be tight.The students are coming for the machine. And, astonishingly, they might win.Super interesting, right? US electoral politics don’t work the same as Serbia’s, but I wonder if there’s a way to inject some aspect of the Student List into US elections?

item.title: Following the Midterms at TPM
item.author: Josh Marshall

item.content:encoded: As we get ready for the final days of the 2026 midterm campaign, I wanted to flag some key parts of our coverage. First, don’t miss our midterms liveblog which you can find on the front page and also at this link. We’re starting with a focus on election interference issues and then we’ll shift toward broader Election Day news and results as we move into next week. Next, the TPM team has done a comprehensive analysis of just who certifies election results in each of the Senate swing states and what funny business they can pull. You can see that here. We also have our take on which 13 races we think will define the midterms, which you can read here. Finally, join us here Tuesday night. For the first time we’re going to be doing live video coverage of election night. Think of it as comparable to what you might see on CNN or MS NOW but with more insight about how to understand the results, what’s happening in key counties and precincts rather than just the toplines and just TPM level analysis. I hope you’ll join us.

item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: We’re going get to Barack HUSSEIN Obama taunting Donny a, I promise. But first, we need to put our Hero of the Day right up top. At a hate-rally in Mississippi two days ago, this loyal, patriotic American had a heartfelt message of undying affection and support for Dear Leader. Let’s give it a listen.“Release the Epstein Files! Shove that ballroom up your fat ass!”How sad is it for Donny that he’s now been reduced to campaigning in such tiny little rinky-dink venues — high school gymnasiums and the like — that it only takes one determined heckler with a good set of lungs to throw the whole event off the rails?Wait, did I say sad? I meant to say . Shoot that shit straight into my veins.Honestly, I think Donny’s already got his beloved Epstein Dance Hall shoved up his fat ass. That’s the only reasonable explanation whatever the hell is going on back there these days.And now, on to the main event. Remember the other day, when Obama thoroughly humiliated Donny by pointing that that the Oval Bordello has been tatted up with so much golden crap that it now ‘looks like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory’?Trump is BIG MAD about Obama saying the White House now looks like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory: “He’s not a smart guy. He's not smart at all ... for you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.”Shut the fuck up, Donny. Grow a sense of humor.So of course, when faced with such an irresistible, thin-skinned piss-baby target, Obama did the only logical thing.“What I said about them being directly responsible for rising prices, they did not argue with that. They did not deny that tariffs were contributing to higher costs per family. They didn’t say anything about that. I accused this administration, based on the facts, that they were engaging in unprecedented levels of corruption, they didn’t say anything about that. The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison. That part didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comments. He took great umbrage. He said I didn’t understand the work of the artisans in the White House. And they mobilized — it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part — they mobilized a whole government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke. The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy. The person who’s supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable. The guy who’s supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation. And reduce interest rates. They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”Come on, we’re supposed to believe that the guy who probably throws a thermonuclear shit-fit when the sommelier bring out the wrong vintage of Lafitte Rothschild — ‘I said the ’75, you peasant, not the ’76, what is wrong with you’ — is chowing down at any place with ‘factory’ in its name?Bessent is the kind of shitweasel who goes ballistic if the valet leaves a fingerprint on the door of his Bentley. He’s not jamming any ‘French-dip cheeseburgers’ down his gullet.As Obama so correctly points out, Scott Bessent has actual, important job that he should be busy with — but instead of doing any of that shit, Donny makes him drop everything to go stand in front of the nearest camera.These are not serious people. They’re all fucking embarrassments. None of Donny’s flunkies have any fucking idea how to their jobs. They have no clue how to fix any of the shit they’ve broken. All they want is to be famous and on TV. Instead of winning the unwinnable war he started, Piss-Drunk Pete Kegstand holds useless photo-ops where he does the shittiest pull-ups you’ll even see. Why? How is that even relevant to anything related to his actual job?‘Gaze in awe at my weak-ass pullups.’ Yay, Pete.The Secretary of Transportation has a reality show that no one watches. The Secretary of Health has a cooking show. Even Dear Leader has his own TV channel. Remember that, the youtube channel that Dear Leader started when the networks held their impotent, one-day boycott of the White House press office? Of course you don’t remember. No one fucking remembers. But it’s still here, watched by absolutely nobody.The only member of the Donnyverse who isn’t super horny to get himself on TV is Marco Rubio. He hides out in who the fuck even knows where he is, because he’s terrified that some reporter might ask him why he’s wearing oversized clown shoes. Check out this shoebox. Can you guess what it is?This is the Ohio venue where Donny held last night’s hate-rally. My god, it’s another tiny little gymnasium. How fucking pathetic. You can really feel the , can’t you? It’s five days before what’s probably the most consequential election of our lifetime, and the President of the United States can’t fill a room that holds three hundred people. Now, remember what I said up top about how in a venue that small, any determined heckler with a powerful set of lungs could derail the whole thing, and make it come crashing to the ground?“Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane! Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane! Butterscotch Hitler! Pumpkin Spice Pedo! Butterscotch Hitler! Pumpkin Spice Pedo! Ah ha ha ha!”‘Pumpkin Spice Pedo,’ how fucking perfect is that? No notes.I also love the way this guy manages to keep filming — and keep heckling — even as he’s wrestled to the ground by MAGA chuds and escorted all the way to the sidewalk by security.This one’s for you, ma’am.Let’s have some more selfies from Ms Spouse’s phone. First, at Harvest On Hudson on December 17, 2025.Have a great Thursday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Mahmoud Khalil On His Time In ICE Detention And The Existential Threat Facing Higher Education
item.author: Sarah Borus
item.content:encoded: I remember the pit in my stomach as I woke up to the texts telling me that Mahmoud Khalil had been kidnapped. I remember the terrifying 48 hours when we had no idea where he had been taken—just that the President wanted to make an example out of him. I remember crying on the phone to my dad, telling him I had lost all hope. It was difficult to relive, and in preparing for this interview, I wanted to do Mahmoud justice.Mahmoud was central to the community of activists at Columbia University. He was the person we looked to for calm and guidance in the midst of upheaval. When he was taken, we all felt his absence. We were mostly kids. We struggled not just with the question of how to push back against the intensity of encroaching fascism and the weight of the federal government's crackdown on free speech, but how to do so without Mahmoud. He knew the university rulebook front and back. He knew all of the administrators and had a friendly rapport with them (or so we thought). He would calm us down when it felt like everything was falling apart. All of a sudden, he was thousands of miles away at a detention center known for inadequate medical care, unsafe food and living conditions, and abusive tactics by guards. And we remained inside the gates of the place that had allowed it to happen, as the retired Homeland Security Secretary, former IDF intelligence officer, and war profiteers who made up the administration and board of trustees wrung their hands and told us they were powerless. Mahmoud’s book is a devastating and essential story of his time in ICE detention, his childhood in Syria, and his experience as a negotiator at Columbia. In typical Mahmoud fashion, he insists that there are people far braver than him, who have made more sacrifices than him. He wants you to know the stories of the men he was detained with. They too were separated from their families and held without any charge.

item.title: Finally, A Good Book About Men
item.author: Grace Byron
item.content:encoded: The past few months, I have experienced multiple male cab drivers trying to get my phone number to take me out on a date. One even stopped his car a few blocks away from my apartment. I have also had men yell "Nice tits" and make obscene gestures at me while driving away. I got a boob job a few years ago, so you could say I was asking for it, but the sheer volume of men who corner me in public would suggest that it’s more than an isolated incident. This kind of harassment is ubiquitous. Still, I love men. I would like them to do better because I do often enjoy their company. I know I have previously panned many books on reforming the coarser sex—you could say we are living in a crisis of bad books about the masculinity crisis. Thankfully, Jon Ronson's is a thoughtful, empathetic work of narrative journalism. His prose is rigorous. No adverb or adjective is wasted. Ronson is a sort of literary Louis Theroux, interested in the ideas and people at the fringes of society. He's explored a number of conspiracy theories, hosted multiple podcasts and radio shows, and wrote a book on cancellation and stigma called So You've Been Publicly Shamed. In , he follows two primary narrative strands: a man who is trying to lure women to his fortress in rural Connecticut, and a man who was shamed online for making video content that involved his kids. Through these stories, he wonders what a more positive version of masculinity could look like for future generations. He is neither proscriptive nor apolitical when considering the lonely destructive capacity of men without an outlet.

item.title: Make no mistake about what the DOJ is doing
item.author: 1axb0hlhpcgirr5f8ame2x9omqpbfmjiqhvhlv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: It is nearly certain to lose its frivolous case against Alaska over certification of the Senate election. And it is threatening to sue Washington State (and lose) in a copycat of the case it just lost in California.All this losing has not deterred the administration from escalating its attacks on our elections. To the contrary, each wave of defeats encourages Trump to propose an even more authoritarian response.It is this escalation in its war on voting that is so troubling.At no point in any of these cases have the DOJ or the White House reexamined their stance. Neither has even entertained the possibility that what they seek to do is illegal, unconstitutional and undemocratic.In the California ruling, the judge observed: “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”Instead of reflecting on these sobering words, the DOJ immediately filed an appeal.When I shared the news of this latest decision and the subsequent appeal, several allies assured me it would be fine because my legal team would prevail. While I appreciate the confidence, a democracy that counts on the federal government losing all of its election cases will not remain a democracy for long.It was one thing to defeat the likes of Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell in the aftermath of the 2020 election. It is quite another to pull off the same winning percentage when the Department of Justice is on the other side.Yet that is where we are once again for the 2026 midterm elections. And those willing to stand up and fight are largely on their own.Sadly, the legal profession, corporate leaders and legacy media have all failed us. They will risk nothing to ensure free and fair elections.The largest law firms stand on the sidelines and look the other way as these court fights play out. Corporate leaders are silent about the attacks on our elections. The legacy media is consumed with both-sides coverage and sanctimonious self-congratulation.The next few weeks are going to be difficult. The lies and threats will intensify.Trump will grow more desperate. DOJ will be further weaponized against Democrats and anyone else standing in Trump’s way.More cases will be filed. The DOJ will lose and appeal. All eyes will turn to the U.S. Supreme Court.I am used to this rhythm. It is my job and my obligation to do my part.But I am warning you now: this is unsustainable.Once this election is over, we must do more to protect democracy and free and fair elections.That means real reforms to how we protect voting rights and how we staff and run elections. The fate of our elections can no longer depend on pro-democracy forces winning every single case in court.We cannot afford to relive this in 2028 and beyond.

item.title: Pumpkins Should Have Gone Extinct
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Plants that produce fruit want to be eaten, because that's how they disperse their seeds. Long, long ago, the ancient ancestor of pumpkins evolved to be eaten by megafauna like mastodons. They were too bitter and toxic for creatures like humans. Besides, they had a really hard rind. Only those large animals could open the fruit, tolerate the taste, and properly spread the undigested seeds around with some handy manure for fertilizer.Then around 12,000 years ago, humans wiped out the mastodons, giant sloths, mammoths, giant bears, and other animals that ate those proto-pumpkins. Those bitter pumpkins weren't appealing to other mammals, so how did they survive to today? They are an evolutionary anachronism, a species that should no longer exist. You might not be surprised to learn that it was because of humans, who do weird things. PBS Eons explains how we got pumpkins even though they should have died out thousands of years ago. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: The Milwaukee Brewers Are The Obvious, Implausible Champions
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: It is difficult to encapsulate the Milwaukee Brewers' first World Series victory, because for all the limiters and qualifiers that suggest they had done the implausible—the payroll, and the market size, and facing the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the "first World Series victory" of it all—they had, in all reality, done the very probable.The Brewers had the best regular-season record in Major League Baseball, with 103 wins. By many metrics, they had the best starting pitcher in baseball, with Jacob Misiorowski. They were rested coming into the World Series, and though no one could know this until the first game in Tampa, they were playing with a seven-game home-field advantage. They swept the Dodgers and then won the World Series in five; for good measure, they also nearly won the one game they lost. It is insulting to the broader picture that the Brewers failed to sweep. No team down 0-3 in the World Series has ever forced a Game 6. If the Tampa Bay Rays ever got close, it was in the manner of one of Zeno's paradoxes: closing in by halves to the possibility of making it an interesting series, and never getting there.However, it would be incorrect to state that the Brewers had done the very probable, because in an MLB postseason, achieving the very probable is very, very difficult. Even the best bullpen in baseball, never mind the third-best, will experience bad days. Hits dry up. Everyone makes an untimely error one time or another. Winning in baseball is one thing, but making it look totally controlled is hard work. Just ask the Los Angeles Dodgers, world-beaters for a decade or so, who failed to beat the world more times than not. On the most recent occasion they did, it required the intervention of several magicians, or at least Miguel Rojas and Andy Pages.

item.title: Jeremiah Chiu (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Jeremiah Chiu, a Taiwanese-American synthesist and composer from Chicago. He took up piano and violin at age five, and went on to play keys in bands (pop punk), leading to an interest in synths. Now based in Los Angeles, Chiu creates fascinating synth compositions, often on interesting instruments. His 2023 album, , was made at the Vintage Synthesizer Museum in Los Angeles. He’s a member of the electro-jazz quintet SML, contributing modular synths to the group’s virtuosic live improvisations (see example on YouTube), or their “five-person dialogues” as he called them. On his new album, , he mixes arpeggiated synth with drum machines, acoustic drums (by Booker Stardrum and Ben Lumsdaine), viola (Marta Sofia Honer), saxophone (Patrick Shiroishi), and more. “A large part of the studio process is experimenting by taking improvisations or other performances and using them as material for new pieces,” he told us. “I also use these samples to re-synthesize things – i.e. as a carrier voice for a vocoder or as an envelope follower or any other idiosyncratic way of taking one thing and using it to transform something else.” A conversation with Jeremiah follows the streaming links.What’s your earliest memory of music?It was very cute. I remember my parents and I would call my grandparents on holidays or to occasionally catch up – I must have been 3 or 4 – and at the end of each call I would sing Stevie Wonder’s “I Just Called to Say I Love You” to them. Because of that, the song has a permanent spot in my memory and life. As a teenager, I remember learning this song to cover in my pop punk band. Maybe it’s time I do a version.What was your first instrument and how did you get started with synths?I started playing piano and violin at age five or so. I took private lessons on both instruments and eventually joined the junior high orchestra as well as a regional youth orchestra in the Chicagoland area. In high school, I decided not to continue playing in orchestra. It’s something I regret now, but at the time, I started learning guitar and bass and wanted to hang out with my peers in punk bands – a pretty normal desire for a highschooler in the suburbs, I assume.Near the end of high school, all of the friends I had were in bands and equally into punk, emo, and rave culture. Chicago House and Detroit Techno were hugely inspirational and analog (vintage) synthesizers were cheap and plentiful. We were playing in emo punk bands – starting to incorporate synths – and also learning how to beatmatch drum machines to tracks on a turntable. At the time, you could buy a synth (something like a Roland Juno-106) for $100. It provided us with the opportunity to try out a bunch of different synthesizers and sell and trade them easily. A friend, Mike Bingaman, lent me his MC-505 Groovebox and that really got me interested in sequencing, programming synths, and connecting the instruments to each other through MIDI and CV/Gate.In retrospect, it was a unique experience to have so many teenagers in a community that was really open to a lot of music and art.What were your first recordings like? What did you use to make them?My sister had this Casio WK-1200 that wasn’t being used. It sat in our dining room, next to the kitchen. When my parents would be fixing dinner, I would sit on that thing and make songs. It had the ability to record up to six parts using internal sounds. So I learned to make a drum part, bass part, chords, and lead parts. It really taught me how to put parts of a song together. I also spent a lot of time making mixtapes by recording snippets of radio onto boombox that had a record function. I still work like this quite a bit, except I use live performance as my “radio.”Once I was in bands, we – like so many people – had a Tascam 4-track recorder and a single microphone. We learned how to record parts and bus them down to single tracks to add more tracks. From there, the evolution went a bit like this: a 16-track minidisc recorder, a Fostex digital recorder, a Compaq computer with Cubase controlled by a 12-track MIDI console, a Pro Tools MBox with that goofy dongle. All of the early recording experiments were done on cassette tape or CD.What early artists/albums were most influential to you finding your own sound?Isotope 217, Tortoise, and the whole “post rock” Chicago scene were and still are huge influences. I’m grateful and honestly in disbelief that I call a lot of those people friends and collaborators now. Beyond the sound of the albums and music, the proliferation of different groups within a community reminded me of other thriving music scenes, like ‘70s Dusseldorf, Cologne, and Berlin scenes and ‘80s downtown New York scenes.I love looking at liner notes and personnel on albums and seeing a rotating cast of similar characters – especially when those relationships traverse mediums. In particular, I remember being in art school and finding out that Steve Reich and Sol Lewitt were close friends. Moments like that blew my mind because I grew up in a culture where everything seemed to have a defined boundary. Music was Genre, Art was Movements. But the actuality was much more fluid, hybrid, and boundaryless.Ultimately, the goal is to participate in, and support a thriving artistic community where artists can come together, be in dialogue with each other and contribute positively to our understanding and experience of the world.What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make it?I work in Ableton. All of the contributors on the album recorded remotely and then I edited and arranged the material. More than once, a drum take would get resampled or sliced and it would form an entirely new track. For me, a large part of the studio process is experimenting by taking improvisations or other performances and using them as material for new pieces. I also use these samples to re-synthesize things – i.e. as a carrier voice for a vocoder or as an envelope follower or any other idiosyncratic way of taking one thing and using it to transform something else.In my modular rig, I have several samplers and oscillators that I use to create percussion and melody. The samplers are all routed via my mixer’s aux send, so at any given moment, I can sample something and work with that.Only recently have I started to incorporate software synths as a way to work out some of the compositions in MIDI before recording them again with analog synthesizers. On this record, I used my modular synth rig, Roland gear (101, 202, 303, 606, 808), Moog Matriarch, and a few sample-based organs or pads that I made. Beyond that, Marta Sofia Honer (viola), Marquis Hill (trumpet), Patrick Shiroishi (saxophone), Ben Lumsdaine (drums), Booker Stardrum (drums), Takako Minekawa (voice & field recordings), and Will Miller (EVI) all contributed to the album.How did your experience with SML affect your solo work?SML has been a great experience in listening and making intentional moves. Josh (in SML) has talked about it as being a mode of self-producing, or live producing. I think what he means is that when we’re playing live, it’s all improvised, but since it’s a performance, we’re balancing risk-taking with intentionality. Every sound each of us brings to the table is a part of a five-person dialogue. However, each of us has the opportunity to shift the conversation as it’s moving, because we all respond.In my solo work, I improvise a lot in performances. This is usually done with live-sampling and sequencing. With sequencers in my modular rig, I often have a sequence sequencing a sequence. To clarify, instead of sending a sequencer a steady clock pulse, I’m sending it a rhythmic sequence. This starts to articulate and move the sequence I’ve written in ways that are unexpected and forces me to listen, adjust, and react. What I’m interested in is having some volatility in the performance. An opportunity to have things go awry that force me to be present.With my previous solo album, , it felt very close to how SML currently operates. It was collection of improvisations that was then edited down into an album. With I intentionally swung the pendulum in the other direction. Instead of build the record based on improvisations, I wanted to compose some pieces from the ground up. Some of the songs were still born out of an improvisation, but I challenged myself to explore the album in a way that I hadn’t been doing with my other groups (SML, Marta Sofia Honer duo, and Jeff Parker Expansion Trio).You’re also a graphic designer and educator. What are some examples, if any, of your work in those disciplines affecting your music, or vice versa?When people ask if there’s overlap between my art, design, and music practice, I always talk about the vocabulary as a way to understand how similar they are. In all of the creative fields, we can talk about composition, narrative, contrast, tensions, rhythmic, dynamics, etc… While we generally pin art and design towards a more visual realm, and music to be more sonic, I don’t really separate them that way. When I make an album, I always approach it like a film, or narrative work. I’m thinking about the pacing from the beginning to the end. I’m thinking about the tension and release and the changes between songs as opportunities to carry a listener through a series of ideas tethered to one larger concept.In a more direct example, some years ago I was commissioned by The Getty Center in LA to create a score for a player piano as part of their performance, Pianographs. The player piano score rolls vertically across the face of the piano as the music is played. Holes punched in the paper scroll activate notes. Because the scroll was such a visual part of the performance, my approach to the composition was to compose the score by drawing images and words onto the scroll. I was less worried about the exact harmony, melody, or counterpoint, and more interested in hearing how these images and text came to life through sound.Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.I’m not sure if Franco Battiato classifies as underrated as he became one of Italy’s most famous singers. However, his early experimental records , , , etc. are all so incredible, and I’m always surprised that they’re not more widely recognized by today’s selectors. Go listen to them!What are you working on next?I feel so grateful to have the support of International Anthem and to be collaborating with so many incredible artists in our wonderful community. In the coming year, I’m continuing the work with SML, Marta, and Jeff Parker in hopes that one or more of those will finish another album. At this very moment, I’m about to send this interview off and record on an amazing track for Marquis Hill.
